Run today it stops with *«Pass the parsed gedcom.json so the tree side can be matched»*.

**The tree export is not on disk and was never meant to be.** `read-gedcom.py` says so in its own header: *«The GEDCOM itself is NOT committed. It carries dates of birth for living people.»* The copy David exported on 16 September has gone from the downloads folder, and **that is the correct state for a file full of living people's birth dates** — it is not a bug to fix.

**So the file offered back to the tree is frozen at 17 September, 494 people**, while the roster has grown to **1,419 rows** — and the growth is exactly the kind this file exists to hand over: *a tailor's household at Kaštelir, a widow at Bakar born about 1734, a carpenter's family at Parenzo, four households inside the Svetvinčenat years no index covers.*

**The remedy, in order, and it starts with David:** export the tree again → `python3 scripts/read-gedcom.py <file.ged> --out <dir>` → `python3 scripts/export-to-tree.py <dir>/gedcom.json`. *Ten minutes of machine time behind one export. Moved from «next» to «blocked», because it was listed as work this archive could do alone and it is not.*

rows.what: Ivan's AutoCluster — found, read, and it proves the three Croatian clusters
rows.note:
**It existed all along.** Eight reports came off this account on 15 September and only five were opened; Ivan's was one of the three still unread in the inbox. Found and read on 16 September.

**94 matches in thirteen clusters, and the first holds fifty people** — inside it, David's entire cluster of twelve plus Račić from his cluster of four. From the father those are one cluster, not three.

**Every cluster David has is now decided by arithmetic.** Clusters **2, 5 and 6** have ten, three and two members in his father's report and **none** in his mother's; clusters 1, 3, 4, 7 and 8 are the other way round. **No cluster has members in both.** Cluster 9 is in neither and is still called unplaced.

[The table](/dna/#autoclusters). This morning the Croatian three were an inference from a pool of surnames. **They are proved.**

rows.what: The Senj cluster's ten trees — walked, and the name to chase is Vukelić
rows.note:
**All ten opened on 16 September. They do not name a common couple**, and the reason is that eight of the ten are shallow — three of them show three, seven and twelve people. The two deep ones, at **3,597 people and 1,521**, do not touch each other on a single named person.

**What they share is a surname pool, and one name carries further than the rest: Vukelić stands in three independent trees.** Prpić stands in two. Behind them Blažević, Pavelić, Krmpotić, Tomljanović, Biondić, Lopac, Katalinić, Rončević, Šojat, Butković, Šolić, Delale — every one a Senj-hinterland Bunjevac name.

**So the next name to chase is Vukelić, not Blažević.** Blažević is the one this family carries and therefore the one the eye goes to; Vukelić is the one that recurs across the trees with nothing else in common. [Written up](/dna/#autoclusters).

rows.what: Findmypast transcripts at scale — 424 of them, not ten
rows.note:
The sweep of 16 September read **ten** transcripts out of 424 publishable records, and every one of the ten paid: a Cosulich bride at Cardiff, a GRO volume and page, three Italian sets closed as Neapolitan.

**An index row gives a name and a year. A transcript gives parents, a parish, a ship, a street** — and for the Italian sets, a note in Italian naming the frazione and the grandfather. The transcript pages are fully client-rendered with no server-side payload, so there is no shortcut: they come one navigation at a time, about five seconds each. **Start with the 277 United States passenger records**, whose transcripts name the town of last residence — which is the question this archive actually has: *which of these six hundred are ours?*

---

**21 September — counted, and the order of work is inverted.**

All sixteen pages harvested: **307 records**, and they are **270 passenger and crew lists, 13 naturalisation petitions, 11 Italians to America, 6 Canadian border crossings, 2 Illinois naturalisation index, 2 passport applications, 2 British & Irish Roots, 1 UK outbound**. [The count is on the search register](/searched/).

**The naturalisation petitions carry «Birth place as transcribed» in the transcript itself.** No image, no order, one navigation — and that field *is* the question this item exists to answer. **Thirteen records answer it outright; two hundred and seventy need a plate each.** So the passenger lists are not the place to start.

**All thirteen were read, and all three households were already here** — Joseph at *«Gallignana, Austria»* (the first of the Eleven to go), Peter at *«Basel, Switzerland»*, and Bruno, Gerda and Richard at Brooklyn under the alias *«de Franceschi or Seedorf»*. **That is a real result: the naturalisation route is exhausted and it added nobody.**

**What is left is the 270 passenger records, one plate at a time**, and they should be attacked by *arrival year* rather than alphabetically — the Istrian and Kvarner departures cluster in 1900–1914 and again in 1949–1956.

**Two traps, paid for.** A full page load in this SPA **wipes `window`**, so a harvest must be dumped out of the browser before navigating anywhere — 307 rows were collected and then lost to a single transcript click. And the Apollo cache (`window.__APOLLO_CLIENT__.cache.extract()`) holds **index fields only**: `Record:` keys carry what the results table shows and `FulfillableItem:` carries nothing but a price, **so there is no bulk shortcut to transcripts**. The subscription does cover them — `remainingLegacyCredits` is null and `isPurchased` is true — so nothing is being spent.

---

**Struck, and the reason is that it was already done by a better source.**

The transcripts do carry *Residence* with no image needed — that part of the plan was right. **But [the Ellis Island sweep already read 1,400 arrivals and 429 recorded residences](/searched/), and found exactly two Istrian in the whole database.** Findmypast's 270 are a subset of the same arrivals.

**And there is no query that shortens the job**: `keywordsplace` matches ports, not residence — Domenico's transcript says *«Residence Ponte Alpi»* and searching *«ponte alpi»* returns **zero**, so *«Fiume: 0»* and *«Istria: 0»* are worthless as negatives.

**What survives is narrower and worth doing: the 1949–1956 arrivals**, which the Ellis Island database does not reach, and where the Istrian *esodo* sits. That is a new item, not this one.

rows.what: The Irish, Scottish and English parish collections — opened, and empty but for Cardiff
rows.note:
**One hit in the whole of them.** Of the 44 record sets the surname touches, the only British parish register holding anybody of the name is **Wales Roman Catholic Marriages**, with the single 1876 entry that started all of this. No Irish, Scottish or English parish register has one.

For a Catholic family of the Adriatic that is what one would expect. It is written down so that nobody opens them again. [The register](/searched/).

rows.what: The 1921 Census and the 1939 Register — searched, and nobody of the name is in either
rows.note:
**Nobody.** The sweep paged out every result for four spellings — 644 records, 44 record sets — and neither collection is among them.

**That is a finding.** The *South Wales Echo* called them «an old Cardiff family» in 1896 and a De Franceschi married a Cosulich there in 1876. **By 1921 there is nobody of the name left in England or Wales.** [The register](/searched/).

rows.what: Search Franceschi in Puerto Rico — done, and the thread is closed
rows.note:
**Done, and it ends the question.** Two of the San Lorenzo women were read in full from the 1920 census: *Cármen Colón de Franceschi*, 23, and *Aurora Cruz de Franceschi*, 25. **Both born in Puerto Rico to parents born in Puerto Rico**, both entered as *esposa*, both recorded by the enumerator as **Black**.

An **Afro-Puerto Rican** family two generations on the island by 1920, married into a surname that reached the Caribbean with the nineteenth-century Corsican settlement. **Not immigrants, and not ours.** [Written up](/findmypast/).

rows.what: Cosulich in the newspapers — behind a bot check, so it is David's to run
rows.note:
**The search is right and the door is shut.** Since 16 September this family has a Cosulich in it — [Emerico married Marietta Cosulich at Cardiff on 26 July 1876](/at-sea/) — and the Cosulich were shipowners of Lussinpiccolo and Trieste. **A Cosulich ship at Cardiff in the 1870s, printed beside a De Franceschi master, is the join this archive is missing**, and the shipping columns are where it would be printed.

**Both routes are behind a bot check.** The British Newspaper Archive answers a security challenge before it will show a result; Findmypast's own newspaper search carries a **reCAPTCHA field on the form**. This archive does not work round bot checks, so the search waits for a person.

**What to search, when you have five minutes**: *Cosulich* on its own, then *Cosulich* with **Cardiff**, then *Cosulich* with **Aquilone**. The 153 articles already read under this family's own name are on [the search register](/searched/); the earliest sixty of them are shipping intelligence, which is exactly the column a Cosulich would appear in.

---

**28 September 2026 — a third route, open and free, and it half-answers the question.**

**Both routes on this item are behind bot checks. A third is not.** *The **[Portal Stare hrvatske novine](http://dnc.nsk.hr/Newspapers/Search.aspx)** carries the Austro-Hungarian shipping columns of «Primorac», answers on `http://`, and has no challenge of any kind.* **This archive did not work round anything; it used a different source.**

**What it gives, and what it does not.**
· **`Cosulich` → 81 hits** — *but they cluster **1900–1925**: «Naša sloga» 1901, «Jutarnji list» 1912 and 1914, «Sušački novi list» 1925, «Hrvat» 1904.* **Not the 1870s shipping intelligence this item wants.**
· **`Cosulich Aquilone` → 0.** *No page on the portal carries both names.*
· **`Aquilone` → 32**, of which **24 are now read** — *twenty naming Defranceschi as master, four more from 1874–75 where the column prints **no master at all**.*

**⚠ So the join is not made here.** *The question — **a Cosulich ship at Cardiff printed beside a De Franceschi master** — is not answered by the Croatian press, and the British half still needs a person.* **But the item can stop saying the search is impossible: one of its three routes is open, and it has been run.**

*Eight «Aquilone» hits remain unread on page 2 and beyond.*

rows.what: The Memphis family — read, named, and pointing at Carnia
rows.note:
**Done.** *Antonio De Franceski*, born **1875 in Italy**, **arrived 1902**, in the 19th Ward of Memphis by 1910 with *Bertha* **born in Germany** and nine children born 1904–1917 — Pietro, Aurora, Alba, Albert, Flora, Estelle, Serena, Juliet, Romeo and a second Anthony. Three censuses, twenty-one records, and **the 1910 sheet spells them «de Franceski»**.

**Born in Italy in 1875 and leaving in 1902 is the Carnian window.** Istria in 1875 was Austria and an American enumerator would have written Austria. It is not proof and the census says no more than «Italy» — **his naturalisation petition would name the town**. [The reading](/findmypast/).

rows.what: Places with no coordinates — four rescued, forty-one named as undrawable
rows.note:
**Done, and the residue is published rather than hidden.** GeoNames files a village too small for its own settlement record under its **church** or its **railway stop**, and this builder was reading only populated places. Reading churches, monasteries, hospitals, stations and localities — and nothing else — put four more on the ground: Mađarevo is a railway stop, Mandalina a halt, Ludina a station, Komarevo a locality.

**A stream or a hill of the same name is not the village and is deliberately left out.** The Glogovnica in the dumps is a river; taking it would have been a wrong dot rather than a missing one.

**Forty-one places carrying 130 volumes still cannot be drawn**, and [the map page now names them](/map/) instead of letting them be invisible. Three are not settlements at all — *Bolnica Dubrovnik*, *Nahodište Dubrovnik* and *Nahodište Split* are a hospital and two foundling houses, and should in the end hang on their towns. The rest need a Croatian source and a person, not another pass of the same script.

rows.what: The Prato fault, swept across every place — six more found, and now zero
rows.note:
**Done. `scripts/place-audit.py` applies the two tests the builders already had** — a place catalogued only by a provider that works one region cannot be outside it, and a place whose own name carries a country cannot be in another one.

**It found six.** *Senja, Sv. Juraj* — the Senj deanery's coastal parish, eight kilometres from the town Hedviga Blažević was born in — was **outside Belgrade**. *Sv. Jakov-Šiljevica*, the old name of Jadranovo four kilometres from Crikvenica, was in **Šumadija**, and so was *Klasnić* of the Banovina. *Krug* was in **Lower Austria**. *Grad* and *Tišina*, both Prekmurje parishes, were in **Dalmatia**.

**Three faults underneath them**: the region box covered only the two Udine providers and now covers all seven; «Sv.» was stripped and never expanded, so GeoNames' *Sveti Jakov Šiljevica* and the catalogue's *Sv. Jakov-Šiljevica* never met; and this builder had never read `data/gazetteer.json`, where a hand-checked coordinate lives with its reason beside it — so a hand fix could not reach the research map at all.

**The audit reports zero.** It changes nothing itself and should be run whenever a place is added. [Correction 91](/corrections/).

rows.what: Publish the Findmypast index itself — done, all 424
rows.note:
**Done.** [The sweep page](/findmypast/) now carries every publishable record: **177 standing on a place** and **247 whose place is a country or nothing**, in two folded lists. A reader can look for their own grandmother instead of being told how many there are.

**The 220 withheld are still withheld** — electoral registers, Social Security index, obituary notices, divorce indexes.

Two names in the unplaced list are worth somebody's eye. **Bosiljka and Josip Defranceski, born 1918 and 1915, crossing in 1954** — Croatian given names under this family's own fused spelling, and a post-war date. And a **Marta Defranceschi, 1922**, which is the given name [the Pićan errand](/errands/) has been trying to settle for a fortnight.

rows.what: The living rule, audited against the built site — no violations in 1,280 pages
rows.note:
**Done, and it found none.** `scripts/living-audit.py` reads the **built HTML** rather than the sources, because the built HTML is the only thing a reader ever sees: **37 people the archive holds as living, against 1,280 pages**, looking for a four-digit year standing in the same run of text as a name.

**Getting to none took three narrowings, and each is a lesson.** The menu lists every page title on every page and one of those titles is a person's name, so the audit reads only what follows the first heading. **No tag may stand between the name and the year** — without that a households row hands the next person's birth year to the one before. And **no sentence may end between them**, because «David Defranceschi. The 1584 plaque…» is prose about a plaque.

What is left is the search index, where the page title *«1948»* sits beside a name in a lowercased string. [On the method page](/method/): a rule enforced at the door should be checked at the window.

rows.what: The naturalisation and passport records — read, and they stop at «Italy»
rows.note:
**The row promised thirteen birthplaces. The transcripts do not carry one.**

Four were read on 16 September — *Giovanni* of Chicago (naturalised 1937), *Giovanni* of Connecticut (passport 1922), *Louis* (passport 1919) and *Tobias de Franceski* (passport 1922). Every one of them gives **«Birth place: Italy»** and nothing finer. Tobias is the exception and only because he was born in the **District of Columbia**.

**The town is on the image, not in the index.** Findmypast holds the images and links them from each transcript, and the transcripts carry the NARA reference that would fetch the same page from Washington — *M1490 roll 1807*, *roll 1008*, *roll 1842*, *M1285 roll 41*.

So the work is a different job from the one written down: **eighteen images to read by eye**, not eighteen transcripts to harvest. Two are [already an errand](/errands/) because a petition is worth ordering whether or not the image reads.

*Corrected the same day it was written, which is the right speed for a wrong plan.*

---

**21 September 2026 — the images are open, and two towns are out.**

**The viewer was never the obstacle.** A Findmypast transcript id for these sets *is* a FamilySearch film and frame — `US_PASSPORT_APPLICATIONS/**007572652**/**00658**/…` — so the plate can be fetched directly and read on a canvas, with no viewer, no filmstrip and no paging. [The route is written down](/searched/).

**Louis De Franceschi was born at Sequals, Province of Udine, on 3 November 1873**; father **Pietro**, dead by 1919; Havre to Washington in February 1907; naturalised 4 October 1915; **cement decorator**, which is the Sequals trade. **Giovanni DeFranceschi was born at Castronovo on 10 December 1876**; father **Francesco**, dead by 1922; Havre to Torrington, Connecticut in April 1903; naturalised at Winsted in 1911.

**And the index was never wrong.** The form asks the father's birthplace in one blank labelled *«(Country.)»*, so *«Italy»* is the whole of that field. The town lives on the applicant's own line, and only on the **naturalized-citizen** form — which is why **Tobias's native-citizen application of 1922 has no town to give, and his father's has Sequals**.

**Still to read: the remaining images**, and the **Chicago naturalisation of 1937**, which is a different series with a different image path.

---

**27 September — the naturalisation series read, and «they all say Italy» was true of four records, not of the set.**

*The 16 September reading took four **passport applications** and found «Birth place: Italy» in every one, correctly, because that form asks the father's birthplace in a blank labelled «(Country.)». **The naturalisation petitions are a different form and they carry the town.** Ten were read today off the transcript, without an image.*

**The towns that came out:**

· **Joseph Defranceschi — «Gallignana, Austria», born 12 March 1892.** *That is **Gračišće**, the parish this family comes out of. Declaration **22660** (Brooklyn, 1912) spells it **«Gaglinana»**; petition **13838**, certificate **1104860** (1915) spells it **«Gallignana»** — the same clerk's office, three years apart, and the second is right.*
· **Gerda De Franceschi — «Hollen, Germany», born 15 January 1913.** *This archive held «1913» off a gravestone and no birthplace at all.*
· **Peter De Franceschi — «Basel, Switzerland», born 12 January 1902.** ***A country this archive has never recorded for anyone of the name.***
· **Giovanni of Chicago, 1937 — «Italy», and nothing finer.** *Checked, and the earlier reading stands: NARA M1285 roll 41 is a Soundex index card, not a petition, so there is no town on it to find.*

**And one document gives a whole household.** *Declaration of intention **284221**, certificate **2-665402**, Brooklyn 1939, names **Bruno** (b. 12 Aug 1907), his wife **Gerda** (b. 15 Jan 1913) and their son **Richard** (b. 2 Dec 1932) on one paper.* **That is a source naming a couple together, so it is the first spouse link written from a record rather than from the direct-line chart.** *Gerda's oath of allegiance follows in 1944, certificate 5742645.*

*Richard is added as a new person and **deliberately not joined** to the `Richard Defranceschi` already on the roster from David's tree, who carries no dates: **nothing links them but a forename**.*

rows.what: Smyrna, 1906–10 — checked, and it stays open
rows.note:
**She appears once in the whole of Findmypast** and it is the consular marriage itself: GRO MCON, volume 788, line 70. The index does not name the groom, and the finder offers **Helen Whittall, Frederick P Wilkinson, Reginald E Turrell** from the same page.

**Unresolved, and left so.** Only a consular certificate would name her father, which is the one thing that could join her to anybody here. [Written up](/findmypast/).

rows.what: Frieda and John at River Grove — one household, four documents
rows.note:
**Done.** *Giovanni «John» De Franceschi*, born **1895 in Italy**: the 1930 Chicago census with *Freedia* and the children *Thersa* and *Ateo*; **naturalised at Chicago in 1937** (NARA M1285, roll 41); **buried 12 April 1951 at St Joseph's Cemetery, River Grove**. Frieda died in 1988 and *Attilio F Defranceschi*, 1925–2010, is almost certainly Ateo.

Every record says «Italy» and stops. **The petition behind the Soundex index names the comune** and is now [an errand](/errands/).

rows.what: The fifth AutoCluster — read, and it cuts the mother's side nine to five
rows.note:
**Opened on 16 September. 96 matches in six clusters.**

**It shares 31 matches with David's mother and 6 with David** — five to one, which is what a relative on her side looks like, because a child inherits about half of what a parent has.

**It splits her fourteen clusters nine to five.** Nine contain somebody the third kit also matches; five contain nobody. 81 of her 103 matches are in a shared cluster, 22 are not. The nine are her mother's family; the five are her father's — and [the father's side belongs to another session](/cheryl-lerena/), so this archive stops there.

**The by-product is what matters here.** Against David's own nine clusters the third kit touches **1, 4 and 8 — and not 2, 5 or 6**, which are [the Croatian three](/dna/#autoclusters). A maternal relative, tested independently, lands in three of his clusters and in none of the Croatian ones. **That is arithmetic on a third person's DNA rather than an inference from a surname.**

Whose kit it is is not published, for the same reason no match's name is.

rows.what: Three documents to order, and each of them names a place
rows.note:
Three documents this archive cannot read from a desk. Two were found on 16 September and answer the same question — **where in Italy** — and the third, found on 17 September, answers a different one: **who was in the house.**

**The Cardiff marriage certificate** — GRO, Cardiff district, **Q3 1876, volume 11A, page 428**. The parish register gave the two fathers and nothing else; the certificate gives both ages, both residences, both **occupations** and the witnesses. If Emerico's occupation is *master mariner*, [the at-sea page](/at-sea/) stops being a collection of sightings. **£12.50, ordered online.**

**Giovanni's Chicago naturalisation petition** — **NARA M1285, roll 41**. Every American record for that household says «Italy» and stops: the 1930 census, the burial at River Grove in 1951, the Soundex index itself. **The petition names the comune.** Antonio of Memphis, born 1875 and arrived 1902, has one too and it is worth asking for in the same letter.

Both are on [the errands page](/errands/) in full.

**The Arolsen CM/1 file** — **3.2.1.1, ref 32110000 058.158**, filed under *Petar Defranceski, born 15 June 1913 at Crikvenica*, and titled in Arolsen's own words *«and of further persons»*. A CM/1 file says where a displaced person was during the war, who was with them, and where they asked to go. **Arolsen publishes online without an account and answers enquiries free.** [Where it came from](/worklist/).

rows.what: Open Nelida Albina's Argentine baptism ark, 6ZP4-29WC — it may not be a de Franceschi at all
rows.note:
David's tree gives **Nelida Albina de Franceschi, born 9 September 1931 at Mercedes**, as Rotilio's daughter, and cites *Argentina, Buenos Aires, registros parroquiales, 1635–1981*, **ark 6ZP4-29WC**. The citation reads *«Entry for Nélida Albina and Federico Nebbia, 30 de noviembre de 1931»* — and in **every** other citation from these Argentine collections the second name is the **father**. On the face of it the record is a **Nebbia** baptism.

It is the only Argentine record ever attached to [Rotilio's story](/the-eleven/), so it decides whether Argentina stays dotted. **Signed out, FamilySearch answers 401 on the ark** — tested 17 September. It needs one click in David's own session.

---

**22 September 2026 — signed in, and the answer is that the account cannot see it.** The ark no longer returns 401; it renders, and what it renders is:

> **«We're unable to show this record. This record can only be displayed on certain accounts. FamilySearch must honor the agreements we have with our partners, record owners, and internal policies.»**

**So this was never a sign-in problem.** The Argentine parish collection is **restricted by its owner**, and David's own account is not one of the accounts that may see it. *A second sign-in will not fix it and should not be attempted.*

**The question stands exactly where it was**: the citation names **Nélida Albina and Federico Nebbia**, and in every other citation from these collections the second name is the father — so on its face the record is a **Nebbia** baptism, and the only Argentine record ever attached to Rotilio may not be his at all.

**What would answer it now:** the **image** rather than the index entry, or the parish register at **Mercedes (Buenos Aires)** direct. *Keep Argentina dotted, not solid.*

rows.what: The Gračišće marriage register for 16 May 1928 — the name of the woman Rotilio actually married
rows.note:
The register already read gives *«Rutilius 3-11-1902, married 16-5-1928»* and this archive took the **wife's name from the 2012 reunion album** — which [turned out to be his sister's husband's surname](/the-eleven/). David's tree still carries an *«Albine Chinkopan, born Italy, died Buenos Aires»* against that same date.

**The register itself names the bride.** One entry, one date, one parish, and it settles a question two pages are currently hedging. Croatian registers of 1928 fall inside the hundred-year closure, so this may be an errand rather than a click.

---

**21 September 2026 — ANSWERED, and the answer reverses this archive's own reading.** FamilySearch full-text, query *Rotilio Defranceschi*, reached **Trieste, Marriage Proclamation Records 1928, Parte II Serie A n. 132**: *«Defranceschi Rotilo … figlio di fu Antonio … e di Valhart Maria»* marrying *«**Cincopan Albina** … figlia di Giuseppe … e di Trompich Maria»*. **He did marry an Albina Cincopan.** The album was right; the correction published here was wrong. Three people added, a trade recorded, and **Trieste added as a place the bride had lived**. See [/corrections/](/corrections/).

rows.what: Recover the ark and image for each of Valentino's Fiume children
rows.note:
The fourteen children were read off the Liber Baptizatorum of St Vitus on 6 September and **no ark and no image number was kept for any of them**. Ten are also in the FamilySearch index and can be re-joined by their household arks; **four — Ignatius Francus Mattheus 1745, Vitus Joannes Baptista 1751, Aloysius Rochus 1754, Rosalia Francisca 1755 — are in no index at all**, so [their pages](/fiume-1626/#valentino) rest on a reading nobody can check. This archive's own rule is that a read is worth what its citation is worth.

**20 Sept 2026 — eleven of fifteen recovered, and the list turned out to be wrong in two places.** Matching the index on the **parents** rather than the children (`q.fatherSurname` across *Defranceschi* / *De Franceschi* / *Franceschi*, keeping only rows with a *Valentin-* in them) returns eleven rows, six of them this household's: **Matheus Franciscus 1739**, **Aloysius Joannes Petrus 1752**, and the burials of **Mattio 1742**, **Antonio 1753** and **Aloysia 1757** — plus **Jacobus Vincentius, baptised 21 July 1757, who was not in the list at all**. His entry was read on the page before it was believed, and **with him Valentino's sons come out at ten**, which is the number the family has always given. Reading the Aloysia frame settled a second thing: the entry is a **burial** and gives her age as **«d'anni 4»**, so she was **born about 1753**, not 1757 — which is just as well, because no mother bears a live child eight weeks after 20 July.

**What is left.** Four children are in no index — *Ignatius Francus Mattheus 1745, Vitus Joannes Baptista 1751, Aloysius Rochus 1754, Rosalia Francisca 1755* — and four more come back on no spelling tried: *Josepha Catharina 1737, Nicolaus Francus 1741, Nicolo 1742, Francisca Joanna Theresia 1742, Maria 1757*. All of them need the St Vitus film read at their dates. **The ark prefixes are the map for that**: `…-W…` frames are the baptism book, `…-QD…` frames the burials.

**Later the same day, the remaining gap closed to four.** Filtering the surname search on a **date range (1735–1760)** instead of on the father's name returns twenty-two rows, and picks up five more of the household: **Josepha Catharina 1737**, **Nicolaus Francus 1741**, **Francisca Joanna Theresia 1742**, and the burials of **Nicolo 1742** and **Maria 1757**. **Eleven of the fifteen now cite an image.** The four that never come back on any spelling or filter are *Ignatius Francus Mattheus 1745, Vitus Joannes Baptista 1751, Aloysius Rochus 1754, Rosalia Francisca 1755* — **exactly the four this archive named as unindexed on 6 September**, which is as good a check on that reading as the index can give. Those four need the St Vitus film at their dates, and that is all this item has left in it.

**Closed the same day — all four were read on the film.** Any ark resolves to a film and frame number through `/service/records/storage/dascloud/das/v2/3:1:<ARK>`, so the eleven indexed children gave eleven dated frames to interpolate between. **Ignatius Francus Mattheus is frame 126, Vitus Joannes Baptista 228, Aloysius Rochus 257, Rosalia Francisca 272** — and every one sat where the 6 September reading said it would. Three of them gave up a birth date that reading had missed: **28 July 1745, 16 August 1754, 3 October 1755**. **All fifteen children now cite an image, and this item has nothing left in it.**

rows.what: Search the Hungarian and German record sets under the Hungarian and German forms of the given names
rows.note:
**Every sweep this archive has run searched the SURNAME.** Nine spellings of it, systematically — *Defranceschi, De Franceschi, Defranceski, De Franceski, Defrančeski, Defranzeschi, Franceschi*, and the two Australian manglings *Zorafko* and *Zdrafko*. That is why the Australian and Arolsen files were found.

**The given name has never been varied once.** Out of 312 rows in the [research log](/research-log/), eight mention searching by a forename and all eight are a hunt for one named person, not a sweep.

**That is a hole with a shape.** Fiume was a *corpus separatum* of the Crown of St Stephen and its civil registration went over to **Hungarian in 1895**: a clerk there wrote **János**, not Giovanni, **József**, not Giuseppe, **Péter**, not Pietro. [Hungaricana](/method/) is free and this archive already uses it. The same for the Austrian sets and **Johann, Josef, Franz, Andreas**. Sixteen Hungarian forms are already sitting in the records here, unrecognised until today — and they got in by accident, not by being looked for. [The seven columns](/your-name/) are a search plan that has never been run.

---

**Run on 20 September, and the answer is a clean methodological finding: for this name the Magyarised forename is a dead end, but the Magyarised word order is not.**

Sixteen Hungarian forms were put to Hungaricana as phrases, surname first as Hungarian requires. **Fourteen returned nothing at all** — *Gyula* (Julius), *Antal* (Anton), *János* (Ivan/Johann), *Bálint* (Valentin), *Vincze*, *Károly*, *Mihály*, *József*, *Miklós*, *Alajos* (Alois), *Tódor* (Theodor), *Lajos*, *István*, *Ede* (Eduard).

**Two returned, and the pair explains the other fourteen.** *«Defranceschi **Ferencz**»* gives **4 hits** — the Fiume harbour master's pension, his orphan Francziska's grace allowance twice over, and a **Budapest directory of 1848**. *«Defranceschi **Péter**»* gives **1**. The rule behind it: the Hungarian state printed its *sentences* in Hungarian and its *service lists* in German, so the surname inverts but the forename mostly does not. **Ferencz is the exception because it is a spelling, not a translation** — Hungarian *cz* for German *z* in Franz.

**The control matters more than the zeros.** Fourteen nils would mean nothing if the method could not produce a hit; *Ferencz* returning four known records is what makes the nils evidence. The sweep was run because [the search log](/research-log/) showed 312 rows in which the surname had been varied nine ways and **the forename never once**.

**And it was not empty.** *Péter* turned up **a fourteenth man for [the imperial roll](/imperial/)** — *«beim Husz. Reg. Nr 8 · Defranceschi Peter Dr · beim Garnisons-Spitale»*, **Militärschematismus 1867**, a regimental physician and the second doctor on a roll that had one.

rows.what: Where a Cardiff crew agreement of 1876–77 actually is — answered: three places, and the ship's number is the key to all three
rows.note:
**Two things are now settled and the third is the whole job.**

**Settled: the crew lists are catalogued to the person, and further back than expected.** *«Ship: Belgravian; Official number: 98611. William G S Nash; rank/rating, Master; age, 57; place of birth…»* — and not only in the 1915 series: **BT 99/1302/37 is 1881** and **BT 99/1718/16B is 1891**, both with name, rating, age and birthplace. This archive's first explanation of the blank — that shipping is catalogued by vessel and year rather than by master — was simply wrong, and is [retracted](/research-log/).

**Settled: the name is not in it.** *Franceschi rank rating* **0**, *Defranceschi seaman* **0**, against **827** for *«place of birth, Italy» master*. The index is dense, so the absence means something.

**Open: Kew holds only a fraction of the nineteenth-century agreements** — the bulk went to the **Maritime History Archive at Memorial University, Newfoundland**. **Emerico married at Cardiff in Q3 1876 and the *Aquilone* cleared the Bute Docks for Guadaloupe on 11 December 1877.** Establish which repository holds Cardiff-registered agreements for those two years, and write to whichever it is.

---

**Answered on 20 September from Kew's own catalogue, and the question had the wrong shape.** It is not *«Kew or Newfoundland»*. It is **three repositories and one number.**

· **The National Archives, BT 99** — its series description says it plainly: *«a **ten per cent sample** of agreements and crew lists (with log-books where they survive) for the years 1861-1938»*.
· **Maritime History Archive, Memorial University of Newfoundland** — catalogued in Discovery as an external holding: *«Registrar General of Shipping and Seamen, crew lists, agreements and official logbooks (**c70% of total**)», 1863-1938*.
· **County record offices in the British Isles** hold the rest — for a Cardiff-registered ship that means **Glamorgan Archives**.

**And the finding aid that resolves which:** **MF17** at Kew, *«Index to location of crew agreements and logbooks of vessels (microfiche)», 1863-1913* — produced, pointedly, **by the Maritime History Archive itself**. Its entries are *«arranged according to the **official number** of the vessel, the vessels are not named»*.

**So the chain is fixed and its first link is missing.** Ship's name → **Official Number** (from the *Mercantile Navy List*) → MF17 → the repository → the agreement, which names master, crew, ages and birthplaces. **Every BT 99 piece in the catalogue is titled by official numbers alone**, which is why searching the surname returns nothing and always will: the index is of ships, not men.

**Which makes [the Cardiff marriage certificate](/errands/) the hinge of the whole maritime thread.** GRO Cardiff, Q3 1876, vol. 11A p. 428. If Emerico's occupation is given as master mariner, and better still if a vessel is named, the Official Number follows from the *Mercantile Navy List* and MF17 says where to write. Without a ship's name there is nothing to look up, in any of the three places.

rows.what: The rest of the British record: 1861–1911 censuses and the GRO for the Cardiff household
rows.note:
**«An old Cardiff family»** is a phrase a newspaper used in 1896 and this archive has never tested against a census. Findmypast's 1921 Census and 1939 Register [hold nobody of the name](/findmypast/), which dates the disappearance but not the family. **The censuses between Emerico's marriage in 1876 and 1911 have not been searched at all** — and the subscription that would do it is already paid for. Kew is not the place for this; the GRO and the census are.

---

**21 September 2026 — searched, and the answer is the other surname.**

**No person of this name, in any spelling, is enumerated anywhere in Glamorgan in any census from 1841 to 1921.** *Defranceschi* and *De Franceschi* return **nothing** across Great Britain for births 1815–1895; the wildcard *Defrance\** returns **no census record at all** in Glamorgan; and the one historic Cardiff hit on *Franceschi\** is a **Franceschini**, a different name.

**The Cosulich are there the whole time** — Swansea 1871, St John Cardiff 1881 and 1891, Barry 1921, Rhyl 1939. **«An old Cardiff family» is the bride's family, not the groom's.** [The reading is on the search register](/searched/) and the household is [set out under Cosulich](/married-in/).

**What is left is the GRO, and it is an order, not a search**: the 1876 marriage certificate (Cardiff Q3 1876, 11A/428) for Emerico's occupation, and the Cardiff birth index of the late 1870s for the daughter who played at the 1896 Exhibition.

rows.what: Read the Crikvenica marriage film end to end — the only Vinodol marriage register on film that reaches 1885–1908
rows.note:
**Begun 17 September 2026, and the survey of the shelf came first because it changed the target.**

**Across the whole Vinodol, one marriage register on film reaches the years wanted.** Ledenice's *Vjenčani* stops at **1882**; Novi Vinodolski's at **1859**; Bribir's at **1858**; Grižane has no marriage film at all. Only **Crikvenica, Vjenčani 1859–1908**, covers 1885–1890 and 1908. If the marriage of **Josip Defranceschi × Anna Kalanj** is on free film anywhere, it is in that one volume — and if it is not in it, the answer is a letter to the parish office at Ledenice or Novi, not another search.

**The film is open and mapped.** 272 images, DGS **2084742**; every image's ark captured from the waypoint API and held in the session scratchpad; full-resolution pages (about 6000 × 4150) reachable directly, and legible. Year anchors read off the pages themselves: **image 61 = 1862 · image 161 = «Godina 1890» · image 200 = 1897**, so 1885–1890 falls at about **images 138–165** and 1908 at the end of the book.

**The honest cost of «end to end».** The archive's own standard is that a volume is not marked read until every page has been looked at. A page is a two-page spread of about four marriages, and the browser returns 800 pixels at a time, so a spread needs three or four looks. **272 images is therefore something like nine hundred reads** — an afternoon, not a minute, and it is the price of being able to put a green mark on that volume and mean it.

---

**20 September: 17 of 272 read, and three consecutive years are now closed end to end.**

**1887, 1888 and 1889 are complete** — images 151–160, entries 1–19, 1–19 and 1–13, with the priest's own closing line on each: *«U Crikvenici dne 31 prosinca 1889. Alexander Car, župnik.»* **Not one Defranceschi in any of them**, in the couple columns or the parents' and witnesses' columns.

**Why those three years and not others.** Anton Rudolf was born at **Klenovica on 20 January 1890**, so his parents **Josip Defranceschi and Anna Kalanj** married before that; **Ledenice marriages stop in 1882**, which leaves Crikvenica as the only Vinodol marriage register on film covering the window. **1887–1889 is the heart of it, and they are not in it.** That does not close the question — 1883–1886 and the first weeks of 1890 are still unread, and they may have married in Klenovica's or Novi's own parish rather than the bride's — but it removes the likeliest three years.

**One gap to go back for:** **1888 entries 16 and 17** fall between images 157 and 158 and have not been seen. The year is otherwise complete.

**The scratchpad was wiped between sessions and had to be rebuilt** — all 272 arks re-derived from the waypoint and **verified against the previous session's record** (image 156 must be `3QS7-899X-R4S`, and it is). `METHOD.md` now carries the rebuild recipe so the next wipe costs minutes.

**The reading method changed and is much better.** The old auto-crop locked onto the film frame rather than the page, because this film's grey base is as bright as the paper. It is replaced by a **fixed left/right split** — each half of the frame drawn into 800×1100 — which doubles the effective resolution and made the hands legible. Two screenshots per image; about 255 images to go.

**And one question for David, which is a scope question rather than a reading one.** The witness column of 1888 no. 18 carries **«Frančić»**. The declared in-scope list at [/name/#scope](/name/#scope) includes **«Franceschich»**, which is the Italianised spelling of exactly that Croatian patronymic of *Franjo*. **Either Frančić is in scope and this film has hits, or Franceschich should not be on the in-scope list.** It cannot be both. *Flagged, not decided.*

---

**20 September, second sitting: 1883 is complete, and a year label had to be corrected before it did any harm.**

**The correction first.** Image 132 was logged an hour earlier as *«Godina 1885»*. Read at full magnification it is unmistakably **«Godine 1883»** — the same flourished hand that had already turned 1888 into 1877 at low resolution. **The digit was re-read, not guessed**, and everything then fell into place: 1882 closes on image 131 with *«Crikvenica dne 31 prosinca 1882»*, so the next year must be 1883. **1883–1886 is images 132–150**, which is four years across nineteen images — the same four or five images a year as the rest of the film.

**1883 is now read end to end: images 132–136, entries 1 to 23, and no Defranceschi.** The year closes with blank ruled rows after entry 23, which is how this register ends a year. The names are the same closed village as ever — Car, Kalnić, Škiljan, Kristofor, Vračić, Bernjac, Škomerža, Kulentić, Matejčić, Manestar — with two outsiders worth noting: **no. 19, Josip Car, a clerk at the royal district tax office at Karlovac**, and **no. 21, Ivan Barac of Grižane marrying Ana Car of Crikvenica**.

**1881 and 1882 were read on the way past** (images 124–131) and are also clean, which was not asked for but costs nothing to keep.

**Read so far: 31 images of 272**, and **1883, 1887, 1888 and 1889 are complete years**. Still to do for David's window: **1884, 1885 and 1886 — images 137 to 150**.

*Method note: the crop is now a magnified window on the left page rather than a whole-frame view, because the couple columns are what carry the surname. The parents' and witnesses' columns on the right page are a second pass, still owed for 1883.*

---

**1883 to 1889 is now read end to end — seven consecutive years, 144 marriages, and not one Defranceschi.**

| year | images | marriages |
|---|---|---|
| 1883 | 132–136 | 23 |
| 1884 | 137–141 | 25 |
| 1885 | 142–148 | 31 |
| 1886 | 148–150 | 14 |
| 1887 | 151–154 | 19 |
| 1888 | 155–158 | 19 |
| 1889 | 158–160 | 13 |

Each year closes in the priest's own hand — *«U Crikvenici dne 31 prosinca 1886»*, and so on — so these are **whole years, not samples**. 1881 and 1882 were read on the way in and are clean too.

**What that settles.** Anton Rudolf was born at **Klenovica on 20 January 1890**; his parents **Josip Defranceschi and Anna Kalanj** must therefore have married by 1889. **Ledenice marriages stop in 1882.** Crikvenica was the one Vinodol marriage register on film that covered the gap, and **the seven years that matter are now read and they are not in it.**

**So the marriage is not at Crikvenica, and the search moves to three named places**: the parish that actually served **Klenovica** — Novi Vinodolski — whose register is the obvious next order; **Ledenice after 1882**, whose later volumes are not on this film and must be asked for from the Matični ured; and **Bribir or Grižane**, the two neighbouring parishes whose people marry into Crikvenica on these very pages. *This is a redirection built on a complete reading, not on a sample.*

**The village these pages describe is worth recording for its own sake.** Ninety-three marriages in four years among **Car, Kalnić, Škiljan, Kristofor, Vračić, Bernjac, Kovrić, Jurinčić, Veljačić, Matejčić, Manestar, Brozičević, Župan** — marrying each other, house number after house number. The outsiders are countable on one hand and each one is an occupation: **Mirko Car, master mariner** (1885 no. 24); **Adalberto Radil, a baker** (1885 no. 26); **Ivan Vinko Grohovac, temporary schoolmaster** from Grohovo by Rijeka (1886 no. 4); **Eduardo Janić of Bakar** (1886 no. 7); **Josip Car, clerk at the royal tax office at Karlovac** (1883 no. 19); and **Marija-Eva Pilz of Gospić** (1886 no. 10), the only German name in four years. **A Defranceschi would have stood out exactly as these do** — which is why the negative can be trusted.

**Read so far: 45 of 272 images.** The declared strength for 1883–1886 is **the couple columns on every page** — both surnames, occupation, house number — plus the parents' and witnesses' columns on image 150. **The parents' and witnesses' columns for the rest of 1883–1889 are a second pass and are still owed**; a Defranceschi could in principle stand there as a father or a witness without appearing as a bride or groom.

---

**Second pass done. 1883–1889 is now read on BOTH pages — every column of every entry — and the name is not there.**

The right-hand page of this register carries **Parentum Nomen** (both sets of parents, with the mothers' maiden names), **Testium Nomen** (two witnesses with their fathers' names and trades), the **celebrant**, the **banns and dispensations**, and the **Observationes**. Twenty-five right pages were read to finish images 132–157; 150 and 158–160 had been done in the first pass. **144 marriages, seven years, four columns of names each, and no Defranceschi anywhere in them** — not as a groom, not as a bride, not as a father, not as a mother, not as a witness.

**That is the strong form of the negative.** A man can marry out of a parish and never appear in its register; he cannot easily be a **father or a witness** there either without leaving a trace. Josip Defranceschi is absent from Crikvenica in all four roles across the whole window in which his son was conceived and born. **The marriage, and the family, were somewhere else.**

**Things the right pages gave that the left ones could not.** The parish had **three priests, not one**: Aleksander Car signs almost everything, but **Vč. g. Mate Škiljan, umirovljeni župnik** — a retired priest — takes services on images 148, 149, 153 and 155, and **Lovro Zenac, kapelan Grižki**, comes over from Grižane for 1885 no. 24. **Two marriages needed military permission** — *«dozvolom vojničke oblasti»*, from Rijeka (1884 no. 16 and 1886 no. 6), which means a serving soldier. And the witness column is where the village's professional class shows up: **Josip Šanvić, obćinski bilježnik** (parish notary), **Mate Car, obćinski pazitelj** and **kr. lučki pazitelj** (harbour watchman), a **trgovac**, and on 1888 no. 12 **Narcisio Kamin, professor of navigation** — a nautical school teacher standing witness at a Crikvenica wedding.

**The scope flag is now on two pages, not one.** Witnesses spelled **«Franić» / «Frančić»** appear at **1888 no. 6** and **1888 no. 18**. The declared in-scope list still contains **«Franceschich»**, which is the Italianised form of that same Croatian patronymic of *Franjo*. **Ruled on 20 September 2026: *«frančić is adjacent, take franceschich off the list»*.** So they are not hits, and **the seven-year negative for 1883–1889 stands unqualified**. *Franceschich* has been moved to the adjacent forms and taken off the drift chart — [correction 110](/corrections/). Twelve spellings are the name; six are adjacent.

---

**Into the second half: 1890 and most of 1891 read, both pages, on the way to 1908.**

**1890 is complete** — images 161–163, eleven marriages, closed *«U Crikvenici 31 prosinca 1890»*. **1891 is read to entry 23** across images 163–167. **No Defranceschi in either year**, in any of the four name columns.

**The village is beginning to leak, and the register shows it.** Where 1883–1886 had five outsiders in four years, 1890–91 already has a bride from **Senj** with the **župnik of Senj himself standing witness** (1890 no. 9), a groom from **Vrbnik on Krk** married by permission of the Vrbnik parish office (1890 no. 11), a man from **Sv. Križ Začretje in the Zagorje** who is a **čuvar na željeznici u Rieci** — a railway guard at Rijeka (1891 no. 14) — and brides and grooms out of Grižane and Sv. Jelena. **The railway and the steamer are pulling strangers into a parish that married itself for centuries**, and that is the context in which a Defranceschi could arrive.

**And the bishop came.** Image 165 carries a seal and a signature across the foot of the page: *«Vidjeno na kanoničnoj vizitaciji dne 20. svibnja 1891 — **Juraj Posilović, biskup**»* — the Bishop of Senj-Modruš inspecting the register in person. It is the second visitation mark on this film; there is another, unsigned, in 1881.

**53 of 272 images read.** 1883–1891 is now continuous and complete except the last stretch of 1891. Still to do: **1892–1908 (images 168–272)** and **1859–1882 (images 4–123)**.

---

**1891 and 1892 complete; 1893 begun. 59 of 272 images.**

**1891 closes at 24 marriages** (images 163–168) and **1892 at 23** (images 168–172), each signed off by Aleksandar Car on 31 December. 1893 is open at entry 5. **No Defranceschi in any column of either year.** **1883 to 1892 is now ten unbroken years.**

**The outsiders have stopped being a trickle.** In 1892 alone: a **joiner from Vrbnik on Krk**; **Dragutin Gaus**, another joiner, married by leave of the **royal Hungarian ministry of defence**; and — the first of its kind in this book — **Marko Pavletić, an innkeeper, marrying Zuzana Rotter of Nádasd in Hungary**, the pair of them entered as **«necatolik»**. A Hungarian Protestant bride in a Vinodol parish register is the clearest sign yet that Crikvenica had stopped being only a village and started being a **resort on a railway**.

**That changes what the negative is worth, and the change runs the right way for this search.** The closed-village argument that makes the 1880s nil so strong gets weaker each year — but the reason it weakens is that **strangers with foreign names were arriving and being written down**. If a Defranceschi ever came to Crikvenica, this is the decade the book would show it. So far it does not.

---

**1893 and 1894 complete, 1895 read to entry 20. 71 of 272 images. Twelve unbroken years, 1883–1894, and still nothing.**

1893 closes at 23 marriages, 1894 at 18. **No Defranceschi in any column of either.**

**The register itself improves from 1894** — the clerk stops writing ages and starts writing **exact birth dates** for bride and groom, which is why these later years would identify a man rather than merely name him.

**And the arrivals keep widening.** A **pharmacist from Kraljevica** (1893 no. 17); a man from **Bag — Karlobag** (1893 no. 14); a bride from **Grosuplje near Ljubljana** whose mother was a **Kropf** (1894 no. 15); a groom from **Lič** with a **railway watchman at Rijeka** standing witness (1894 no. 16); a wedding performed **at Kraljevica** by its own chaplain (1895 no. 19); and a **post-and-telegraph official from Gospić** married with **Tomislav plem. Budisavljević** — a nobleman — as witness (1895 no. 20).

*The parish is now marrying pharmacists, telegraph clerks, railwaymen and a Slovene bride. It is exactly the population a Defranceschi would have belonged to, and he is not in it.*

---

**1896 and 1897 complete, 1898 read to entry 24. 89 of 272 images. Fifteen unbroken years, 1883–1897.**

1896 closes at 22 marriages, 1897 at 26. **No Defranceschi in any column of either.**

**One old error corrected on the way past.** A previous session logged **image 200 as «1897 nos 1–2»**. It is **«Godina 1898» nos 1–5** — the names it recorded (Zenić/Kovrić, Župan/Župan) are right, **the year was misread**, the same flourished-digit trap that turned 1888 into 1877 and 1883 into 1885. *That is the strongest form the negative can take. The parish was no longer closed; it was pulling in exactly the kind of Italian-named tradesman this family produced. Fifteen years of it, and the name does not appear once.*

**1898 and 1899 complete, 1900 read to entry 20. 100 of 272 images — and the film is now more than a third read.**

1898 closes at 24 marriages, 1899 at 32. **Seventeen unbroken years, 1883–1899, and the name is in no column of any of them.**

**A second bishop signs the book.** Image 210: *«Vidio na kanoničkoj vizitaciji u Crikvenici dne 20. svibnja 1899. **+ Antun**»* — **Antun Maurović**, Posilović's successor at Senj-Modruš. That is two episcopal visitations caught in this reading, 1891 and 1899.

**By 1899 the register has become a list of masons.** Page after page: *zidar, zidar, zidar*. The Grand Hotel and the villas were going up and the parish was marrying the men who built them — with a **brewer**, a **tinsmith**, a **gendarme**, a **butcher**, an **innkeeper** and a servant named **Prohaska** among the witnesses.

**Which is the whole point of reading it.** *Zidar* is the trade **Anna Kalanj's own brother** followed, and it is the trade an immigrant Italian-named craftsman would have followed too. Seventeen years of masons at Crikvenica, and not one of them is a Defranceschi.

**1900, 1901, 1902 and 1903 complete. 113 of 272 images — twenty-one unbroken years, 1883–1903.**

1900 closes at 24 marriages, **1901 at 21, 1902 at 26, 1903 at 28**. **No Defranceschi in any of the four name columns of any of them.**

The groom is a **Blašković**, so it is an observation, not a find; but it shows the clerk *did* write Italy in this column when Italy was the answer, which is one more reason the seventeen-year silence on the name means what it says.

## The second half of the film is finished. 1883 to 1908 is read end to end, both pages, and the name is not in it.

**1908 closes at 33 marriages** (images 262–268), and image **272 is the film's own closing target**: *«ŽUPA CRIKVENICA · HRVATSKA CROATIA · MATIČNA KNJIGA VJENČANIH 1859–1908 · ITEM 1 · project CRO 00008 · roll 28»*. **There is nothing after it.**

**Twenty-six consecutive years — 1883 to 1908 — every entry, every column.** Roughly **560 marriages**, each carrying a groom, a bride, four parents with the mothers' maiden names, two witnesses with their fathers' names and trades, the celebrant and the dispensations. **No Defranceschi stands in any of those roles, in any year.**

**The last three pages are not entries at all, and they are worth having.** Images 269–271 are blank ruled pages with **loose certificates pasted onto them** — the parish's own working papers, kept in the back of the book:

- a **freedom-to-marry certificate of 16 November 1868** for a Tomas Škrolin-Lončar of Crikvenica, signed **Josip Medvedić, crikvenički vikar**;
- another of **22 November 1869** in the same hand;
- a medical clearance for a Mihovil Car, *«Crikvenica 20/4 66»*;
- and, dated **22 April 1866**, a note about Ludoviška Car of Crikvenica signed **«Katarina Šuvčić, babica»** — **the village midwife, in her own handwriting**. She is not a name this archive was looking for, and she is exactly the kind of person a parish register almost never lets you hear from directly.

**And one entry that shows how far the parish would reach when it had to.** 1908 no. 17, Mate Brnjičić and Ljuba Car, was married on a **papal brief — *Breve Apostolicum*, Roma, 10 February 1908** — dispensing an impediment of affinity in the collateral line. Beside it, on the same page, sits an entry **struck through diagonally and renumbered**: the clerk cancelled a marriage he had written down and gave the number to the next couple.

**What is left.** The first half — **images 4 to 123, the years 1859 to 1882.** Those years matter less for Josip and Anna, who cannot have married before about 1883, but they are the years in which **a Defranceschi grandfather could have come and gone**, and the standard for marking this volume read is every page. The reading continues at image 4.

**The first half is open, and the book turns out to be in Latin.**

Images 4–8 are the film's own front matter and they are worth keeping, because they give the citation this volume has never had on the site: the register is **Povijesni arhiv Rijeka 275 (K4), inv. 110**, *Matične knjige rimokatolika, župa Crikvenica, Matična knjiga vjenčanih (1859–1908)*, filmed at the **Hrvatski državni arhiv in Zagreb on 14 November 1996** by an operator named **Anita Kekić**, project CRO 00008, roll 28.

**From image 9 the register begins, and every entry to at least 1861 is written in Latin.** *Leopoldus, Josephus, Stephanus, Bartholomaeus*; *agricola* for every trade; *Ter promulgati* in the banns column; dispensations *«in tertio gradu consanguinitatis»*. **That changes what the eye is looking for.** In these years the name would be written **de Franceschi, Franceschi** or **Defranceschius** — the Latin nominative — and not the Croatian form the later pages would use. The reading is being done with that in mind.

**1859 closes at 15 marriages, 1860 at 12** (*«Sequitur Annus 1861»* in the priest's hand), and 1861 is open. **Nothing so far.** Two names were magnified to be sure they were not ours and were not: a *Kostrulja* that looked briefly like a *franč-* form, and a groom whose origin appeared to read **Zara** and reads, enlarged, **«Parochia Selcensis»** — the parish of Selce.

**FamilySearch has flagged these pages «WATER DAMAGE / OŠTEĆENO OD VLAGE»**, and the flag is honest: the ink is pale and the margins are cockled. They are still legible.

**1861 and 1862 complete; 1863 read to entry 12. Images 4–30 done.**

1861 closes at **21** marriages, 1862 at **21**, each signed off in the priest's own Latin — *«Sequitur Annus 1862»*, *«Sequitur Annus 1863»*. **No Defranceschi in any column of either.**

**Three names were magnified rather than guessed at**, because in a Latin hand a *franc-* stem is exactly what a hurried eye invents. 1861 no. 11 looked like **Frančić**; enlarged twice, the surname wraps across two lines as **Fra-ssich — Frašić**, which is neither in scope nor adjacent to it. The other two resolved the same way.

**What these pages give besides the negative.** The trade column, which by 1900 is nothing but *zidar*, in 1861 says **agricola** for almost every man — and then begins to admit **nauta**, a sailor. The religion column, uniform for fifty years afterwards, carries in 1862 no. 10 a second line reading **«Cath. Graeca»** beside *Rom. Cath.* — the only non-Latin-rite marking in the book so far. Brides and grooms come in from **Selce, Grižane, Zagorje, Sv. Helena** and once from **Parochia Segniensis**, the parish of **Senj** — which is this archive's other line. And the dispensations are granted not by a chancery but **«ab Excellentissimo ac Illustrissimo Domino Episcopo»**, the bishop in person, for marriages inside the third and fourth degrees of consanguinity: a village marrying its cousins, and the bishop signing it off year after year.

**1863, 1864 and 1865 complete; 1866 read to entry 8. Images 4–44 done.**

1863 closes at **28** marriages, 1864 at **19**, 1865 at only **8** — the thinnest year in the whole book. Each is signed off *«Sequitur Annus …»* over the name of the parish priest, **Stanislaus Katnić, župnik**, and image 35 carries an audit line across the head of the page: *«Presentes Matriculae revisae … In Crikvenica die 10 Oct. 1863 — Venceslaus Car, curatus.»* **No Defranceschi in any column of any of them.**

**And in 1865 the first Italian name in this register finally appears — in the bride's column, and it is not ours.**

1865 no. 7, read at magnification because the hand is small: **«D. Anselmus Susanich, Comitatus Humani Judicii Districtus Vinodolensis Scriba»** — clerk of the **Vinodol district court** — of **Kostrena Sveta Lucija**, marrying **Maria-Anna Montanari**. One of the witnesses is **Antonius Sokol, negotiator**, a merchant. In a book where every other man on the page is an *agricola*, this single entry brings in a court official, a merchant and an Italian surname, all at once.

**That is the shape of the evidence, stated plainly.** When somebody of that kind married at Crikvenica, the register wrote down his office, his district and his wife's Italian name in full. It had the vocabulary and it used it. **It never had occasion to write ours.**

*Two more near-misses were magnified rather than guessed at and both dissolved: 1865 no. 8 looked like a **Franc-** form at reading size and is **Joannes Ivančić**; and an earlier one resolved to **Frašić**. That is now four such checks in the first half, and every one of them has come back a different name.*

The trade column has begun to move: alongside *agricola* it now admits **nauta**, and twice **c.r. miles** — a serving imperial-royal soldier married under **«indulto auctoritatis militaris»**. Witnesses come from **de Schola Selcensi**, the Selce schoolhouse. One marriage of 1863 was celebrated **«in parochiali Ecclesia Selcensi ad S. Jacobum»**, in the church of St James at Selce.

**1866 complete; 1867 read to entry 37. Images 4–58 done — a fifth of the first half.**

1866 closes at **20** marriages. 1867 is already at **37** and still running, the busiest year yet in this half of the book. **No Defranceschi in any column of either.**

**The parish is going to sea.** From 1866 the trade column stops saying only *agricola*: entry after entry now reads **c.r. nauta** — an imperial-royal sailor — or **c.r. miles**, and their marriages carry *«cum indulto c.r. auctoritatis militaris»* or the leave of the **Inclytus Comitatus Fluminensis**, the county of Rijeka. In 1867 alone, seven grooms are serving men. And 1866 no. 12 brings the first ship's officer into the book: **«D. Thomas Brozović, Marinae capitaneus»** of **Bakar**, married by Bakar's own parish priest.

**One page is not a record at all.** At the close of 1866, image 48, the priest has written across the blank remainder of the spread, in a clear hand and much larger than the entries: **«Crescite, et multiplicamini; et replete terram. — Gen.»** — *Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.* Then, beneath it, *«Sequitur Annus 1867»*.

*A fifth magnified check: 1867 no. 10 read as **Franich** at reading size and is **Dračić**. Five checks in the first half, five different names, and none of them ours.*

**1867, 1868 and 1869 complete; 1870 begun. Images 4–68 done.**

1867 closes at **37** marriages — the busiest year of the first half — 1868 at **21**, 1869 at **28**. **No Defranceschi in any column of any of them.**

**The book changes clerk at 1868 and the change is worth noting for anyone who reads after me.** From January 1868 the hand is smaller and rounder, bride and groom are written on separate lines, ages are given as plain numerals instead of *«An. 24»*, and the religion column is spelled out in full — *Romani Catholici*. **Rochus Katnić, cooperator** signs the first year of it; then **Theodorus Marijan**, **Matthaeus Butković**, and from late 1869 **Alexander Car, parochus**.

A merchant from Rijeka and a Slovene bride, in a parish that otherwise married Car to Car. *Again: the register knew how to write an Italian name. It wrote this one.*

**The Genesis line is not a one-off.** It appeared across the blank foot of 1866; it appears again at the close of 1869, this time split over both halves of the spread — **«Crescite et multiplicamini … et replete terram»** — before *«Sequitur Annus 1870»*.

**And the sea keeps taking the men.** *Miles marinus*, *miles maris*, *nauta* — 1869 has four of them in twenty-eight marriages. One witness of 1869 is named in full for the first time: **Joannes Stephanus Mažuranić, ludimagister in Crikvenica**, the village schoolmaster.

## The two Italian families of Crikvenica turn up as witnesses — and that is the sharpest form this negative has taken.

**1870 complete at 25 marriages; 1871 read to entry 11. Images 4–76 done.**

On **10 January 1871** the witnesses to a Crikvenica wedding are, in the priest's own words and confirmed at magnification: **«Emericus Benedetti, mercator in loco, & Eugenius Montanari».**

Both names have been met before in this reading, and both arrived from outside:

- **Montanari** first appears in **1865**, when a Maria-Anna Montanari marries the clerk of the Vinodol district court;
- **Benedetti** in **1868**, when Antonius Benedetti of **Fiume**, a merchant, marries a Slovene bride from Carniola.

**By 1871 they are no longer passing through.** Benedetti is *mercator **in loco*** — the merchant *of this place* — and the two of them stand together at a village wedding, which is what settled families do. The register names them, gives their trade, and states their residence.

**This is the strongest form the argument can take in the first half of the book.** Crikvenica in the 1860s did receive Italian-named incomers; it kept them; it wrote them into the register as grooms, as brides, and as witnesses, with occupations attached. **The parish had both the vocabulary and the occasion. Across 1859–1871 it never once had cause to write Defranceschi.**

*Also on these pages: 1870 no. 16, magnified — **Dominus Vitus Lenčić, localis scholae magister**, of **Lokve**, marrying Maria Magdalena Planinz. The village schoolmaster, another outsider with a profession, another name written down in full.*

**A third bishop signs the book — and this one is the earliest.**

Image 79, across the foot of the 1871 spread: *«Praesentes Copulatorum Matriculas … Nos in Crikvenica occasione Nostrae Canonicae Visitationis revidimus et approbavimus. Sic in Crikvenica die 13ª Octobris 1871.»* — **Venceslaus Soić, Episcopus Segniensis et Modrusiensis**.

That makes **three episcopal visitations** caught in this reading of one volume: **Soić in 1871**, **Posilović in 1891**, **Maurović in 1899**. Each time a bishop of Senj-Modruš sat down with this book, went through it, and signed that he had. *Whatever else is true of this register, it was inspected — which is part of why the silence in it can be trusted.*

**Images 4–80 done; 1871 read to entry 25.** The trades keep widening: 1871 alone has a **sutor** (cobbler), a **pictor** (painter) from Selce, three serving soldiers, and a **nauta of Portoré** — Kraljevica under its Italian name.

*A sixth magnified check: 1871 no. 15 read as a possible *Franc-* form and is **Matthaeus Franović, sutor**. Six checks in the first half, six different names. And 1871 no. 14, first read as «Istria», is **«Sponsus Portoregensis»**.*

**1872 and most of 1873 read. Images 4–86 done. 1872 closes at only 10 marriages — the thinnest year since 1865.**

**Three entries on these pages are worth having, and one of them puts an Italian surname and Ledenice on the same line for the first time.**

**1873 no. 8, magnified twice: «Pius Devalle, sutor»** — a cobbler — his origin written **«Sponsus Ledena[ice]»**. An Italian-surnamed shoemaker **out of Ledenice**, marrying at Crikvenica in February 1873. *He is not ours, and nothing here suggests he is.* But Ledenice is where **Anna Kalanj** was baptised in 1864, and this is the first time in the whole reading that an Italian name and that village appear together. It is logged for what it is: a fact about the place, not a link.

**1873 no. 9, magnified: «Dominus Josephus Pauricchi × Maria Braitenfeld», married *in articulo mortis*** — at the point of death — the union afterwards **ratified by the Ordinariate on 3 April**. A third Italian-form surname, a German one beside it, and a Ragusa connection in the parents' column. The parish register recorded even this, a deathbed marriage of two outsiders, in full.

**And Benedetti is still here.** He witnesses **1872 no. 7** and again **1873 no. 8**, each time written **«mercator in loco»**, once alongside a second merchant, **David Mansanari**. From 1868 to 1873 the same Italian merchant family keeps appearing, and the clerk keeps naming it.

*Also on these pages: **Josephus Jelinić, financiarius**, a revenue officer of Selce, married under indult of the **Supreme Financial Directorate** dated 11 November 1871, with **Vitus Cukić, officialis financiarius** standing witness. The Austrian state is now inside this village register too.*

**1873 and 1874 complete; 1875 begun. Images 4–94 done — the first half is two-thirds read.**

1873 closes at **19** marriages, 1874 at **23**. **No Defranceschi in any column of either.**

These are quiet years in the book and the entries are almost all Car, Brnjac, Župan, Matejčić, Benić, Ivančić and Jurinčić marrying each other across the villages of **Dolac, Draga, Supera, Sopaljska** and **Ludvić** — the same closed circle the 1880s pages showed. The one thing that keeps changing is the witness column, where the parish's small officialdom is now named: a **tabernarius communalis in loco** — the village innkeeper — a **miles pensionatus**, a communal officer, and beside them the merchants **Benedetti** and **Mansanari**.

**Remaining: images 95–123, the years 1875 to 1882.**

## The Montanari, four times across eleven years — and a correction to my own log.

**1875 closes at 19 marriages, 1876 at 23** — the priest writes the total himself: *«Anno 1876 copulati fuere 23. Sequitur annus 1877.»* **No Defranceschi in either.** Images 4–104 done.

**1876 no. 20, magnified: «Dnus Jacobus Pezelj, capitaneus maritimus» — a master mariner — marrying a daughter of DAVID MONTANARI.** The parents' column gives it plainly: *«Dftus Laurentius Pezelj & Maria nata Zelenčić — David Monta[nari] & …»*

That is the **fourth** appearance of this one Italian family in the volume:

| year | the entry |
|---|---|
| 1865 | **Maria-Anna Montanari** marries the clerk of the Vinodol district court |
| 1871 | **Eugenius Montanari** stands witness beside Benedetti, the merchant *in loco* |
| 1873 | **David Montanari** stands witness, *«mercator in loco»* |
| 1876 | **David Montanari's daughter** marries a master mariner |

**A correction to my own reading, made before it did any harm.** The 1873 witness I logged as *«David Mansanari»* is **David Montanari** — the same man, read properly at magnification. The scratchpad log carries the correction.

**This is what a family that actually lived in Crikvenica looks like in this book**: it arrives, it is written down with its trade, it witnesses its neighbours' weddings, and it marries its daughter off to a ship's captain — and the clerk records every stage. **Eighteen years of the register have now been read on both pages, 1859 to 1876, and our name has not once been written in any of them.**

**Remaining: images 105–123, the years 1877 to 1882.**

## The register changes language in January 1878 — and that closes the last gap in the reading.

**1877 closes at 16 marriages**, signed off *«Sequitur annus 1878. Crikvenica 31 decembris 1877. Alexander Car»*. **No Defranceschi.** Images 4–110 done; **thirteen images left.**

**At the head of 1878 the book stops being Latin and becomes Croatian.** *«Ljeta Gospodinova 1878, dne … siečnja»*; **poljodjelac** where it said *agricola*; **Rimo Katolik** spelled out; ages as *«zaručnik 20 godina, zaručnica 22 godine»*; status *«neoženjen / neudata»*. **Aleksandar Car** now signs as **župnik**, not *parochus*, and the observations cite the **Senj Ordinariat** and the Hungarian ministry in Croatian.

**Why this matters for the search, and not only as a curiosity.** The first half of this volume was read looking for **de Franceschi / Defranceschius** — the Latin nominative. From 1878 onward the same eye must look for **Defranceschi / Defranceski**, the Croatian form that the 1880s and 1890s pages use. **The changeover happens inside this reading, and both forms have now been searched for in the years where each was the one the clerk would have written.** There is no seam in the evidence where a differently-spelled name could have slipped through.

**And in 1878 the trade that ends this book begins.** 1878 no. 7: **«Mate Kristofor, zidar»** — the first **mason** in the register. By 1899 nearly every groom on the page is a *zidar*; here is the first of them.

*Also on these pages: **Mate Matejčić, domobranac** — a Croatian home-guardsman, married under leave of the royal Hungarian ministry, the state and its languages arriving together.*
