**So the answer to the question as asked is: no.** Giuseppe is **not** a sixteenth child of Valentino. He belongs to a **second Defranceschi household** at Fiume, and **Helena in 1772 and Ignatio in 1774 were the other household standing for its kin** — which was always the better reading of a habitual godmother.

**Marking this done and opening the question it leaves.** How **Joannes Baptista** and **Valentino** are related is now the join that matters, and it is answerable: their marriage entries are on **this same reel**, in volume 1's **marriages of 1734–1753**, and a marriage entry names a father and usually a birthplace. That is item **143**.

rows.what: How are Joannes Baptista and Valentino Defranceschi of Fiume related?
rows.note:
**Two Defranceschi households baptised at Fiume in the 1740s, and nothing yet connects them.**

**Valentino × Helena** — *«venuto dalla Carnia»*, citizen of Fiume in 1739, **sixteen children 1737–1757**.

**Joannes Baptista × Magdalena** — styled *D.nus*, baptising **Josephus Aloysius on 29 May 1748** (film 005497925, image 150). A **widower by 9 December 1771**, when he marries **Catharina de Benzoni** (volume 2, image 293), with indexed children by her in **1773** and **1776**. **Josephus Aloysius is almost certainly the Giuseppe who heads the Rijeka chain**, which makes this household the trunk of twenty-six indexed descendants, not a footnote.

**He is not Valentino's son.** The only *Joannes Baptista* among Valentino's sixteen was baptised in **1751** and cannot father a child in 1748. Brother, cousin, or no relation at all — the register has not said.

**Why it is worth a name:** if they are brothers, the Rijeka chain hangs off **Carnia** and joins the Mione line this archive already holds. If they are not, Fiume held two unrelated families of the name and a great deal of this archive's Kvarner material has been read as one thing when it is two.

**The read, precisely.** **Film 005497925, volume 1**, which carries **marriages 1734–1753** from about **image 171** — image 171 is already known to show marriages of 1738. **Joannes Baptista × Magdalena must marry before May 1748**, so the window is **1734–1748**, and **Valentino × Helena marry before November 1737**, so they are in the same run or just before it. A Fiume marriage entry names **the father of each party** and usually **where he is from**. **Two entries would settle it.**

*Cheaper still if it works:* volume 2 carries **marriages 1753–1776**, already partly read for 1769–1772. Nothing there bears on this, so the read is volume 1's marriage section and nothing else.

**20 Sept — one of the two marriages is found.** Walking the marriage run backwards from image 189 (*October 1746*) through 170 and 169 to **168R**, second entry:

> «Die 28 Februarij 1737. D.num **Valentinum de Franceschi ex Carnia**, et **Elenam Surcho** junxit in matrimonium D.nus Petrus Eustachius Sauss Canonicus, præsentibus testibus Nob. D.no Petro Petrini et Nob. D.no Antonio Moretti.»

**«Ex Carnia» is now primary**, two years before the citizenship of 1739, and Valentino's wife has a maiden name for the first time: **Elena Surcho**. *(Initial S or Z; given as read.)*

**But the entry names no father** — Fiume marriage entries of this decade give the celebrant and the witnesses and stop there. So **this join will not be made by filiation**. It will be made, if at all, by **finding Joannes Baptista × Magdalena in the same run and seeing whether the clerk writes «ex Carnia» over him too** — and, better, by whether their witnesses are the same men.

**Read so far:** images **168, 169, 170, 189**. **Unread: 171–188** (1738–1746) and **190–205** (1747–1753). Joannes Baptista must marry **before May 1748**, so **171–190** is the window, and it is **twenty frames**.

**20 Sept — the Fiume marriage run is now read end to end, and the answer is a nil that moves the item.** **Images 168–191, both pages, November 1736 to February 1748.** In twelve years there is **one Defranceschi marriage**: Valentino's own. **Joannes Baptista × Magdalena are not in it.**

Their son was born **24 May 1748**, so if they had married at Fiume they would be inside that window. **They married somewhere else** — exactly as their son Giuseppe would, and exactly as an incomer does.

**So this item leaves Fiume.** Kobler's claim is that a **Giovanni Battista De Franceschi came to Fiume from the Contea di Pisino intorno al 1740** and was *«senz'altro»* of the Gologorica family — **this archive's own line**. His pedigree adds that the man **studied at Fiume** and **married a lady of the D'Agnese family**.

**The test is now a single fact: Magdalena's maiden name.** *D'Agnese confirms Kobler and hangs the whole Rijeka chain off this archive's own line. Anything else kills it.* And the place to find it is **the County of Pazin's registers, which run from 1582 and this archive has never opened**, not Fiume.

**Incidental, and worth having:** Valentino stands **witness** at a Fiume wedding on **28 February 1740** (image 175L), three years to the day after his own — an occurrence in no index. And a **near-miss is retired**: *«Perill.ri D.no Josepho **Defranchi**»*, witness on image 187R in December 1745, is **de Franchi**, a different surname.

**20 Sept, scoped — and the shelf is shorter than the question.** Of the collection's 43 Istrian parishes, only **two** in the County of Pazin have marriage books covering **1740–1748**: **Pazin** (1656–1852) and **Tinjan** (1703–1896). **Gologorica, Gračišće, Pićan and Žminj are not in the collection at all** — and Gologorica is the house with 1711 over the door.

**So a nil at Pazin and Tinjan does not disprove Kobler.** It would mean the entry is in a book that cannot be opened from here, which is an errand, not a read. *Do not let a negative close this item.*

**Tinjan first.** Darovec, quoted on this site already, puts the Friulian-Carnian stratum in *«Pazin, Pićan, Gradišće, Žminj and Tinjan»* — and Tinjan is the only one of the five that is filmed.

**Pazin is enumerated and anchored, ready to run:** waypoint `9R26-16F:391644801,392372801,392373301`, **396 frames**, arks saved to `scratchpad/pazin/arks.lst`. **Index 134 = January 1741. Index 142 = 1746. Index 160 = October 1747 – January 1748.** **Read frames 128–165.** *The volume binds three date-runs together, so anchor by reading and never by interpolating across them.*

**20 Sept — Tinjan read, and it is a nil.** **Marriages 1703–1896**, frames **9–13**, both pages: **1733–1735 and 1741–1749**. **No form of the surname anywhere** — not groom, bride, father or witness. The grooms are Červar, Milinarić, Antolović, Šubić, Smokovac, Dobrila: **a Croatian village marrying its own**, with Italian names appearing only as the notaries who witness everything.

*That is worth having:* it says an incoming Carnian family is **not** quietly marrying into Tinjan in these years, which the Darovec quotation might have led this archive to assume.

**Gap: 1736–1740 was not located.** Frame 9 ends 1735, frame 10 opens «Conjuncti sub Par.o Joanne… 1741». The volume already runs out of order, so those years may be elsewhere in it. **A marriage up to 1747 is covered; 1736–1740 is not.**

**Still open, in order:** Tinjan **1736–1740** if it exists in the volume; then **Pazin marriages, frames 128–165** (arks in `scratchpad/pazin/arks.lst`). **And neither can close this item**, because Gologorica, Gračišće, Pićan and Žminj are not filmed here — reaching those is an **errand**, not a read.

**⚠ 20 Sept, later — the Pazin frame window published above is WRONG. Do not use it.** The years read as **1741 / 1746 / 1747** at frames 134 / 142 / 160 are **1711 / 1716 / 1717**: this clerk's **4** and **1** are not distinguishable at page scale. **Frame 143 writes 1717 twice cleanly**, which cannot sit eight frames after 1746.

**Re-anchored, all read:** **143 = 1717**, **178 = 1733**, **198 = 1742**, **200 = blank leaf**, **205 = a microfilm resolution target**, i.e. a volume boundary. **≈ 2.2 frames to the year.**

**The window for 1740–1748 is frames ≈194–204**, and it runs into the boundary at 205 — so check whether the last years continue in the section after the target. **Eleven frames and a join.** Arks 175–234 are in `scratchpad/pazin/arks175.lst`; 0–179 in `arks.lst`.

*A correction is published for this. When anchoring by date heading in this hand, cross-check every year against a neighbouring frame — and check that the run is possible before writing it down.*

**20 Sept — Pazin read end to end, and it is a nil. The online shelf for this question is exhausted.**

**Frames 194–199 (Dec 1740 – Nov 1742) and 208–216 (1743 – Nov 1748)**, both pages each. **No form of the surname in any role.** The couples are Sgrablich, Mattesich, Cerovaz, Brattulich, Sironich, Mogorovich — an Istrian town marrying its own — and the Italian and German names belong to the Praepositus and the chaplain who officiate.

**The volume is three filmed items on one reel.** The 1656– run **stops at November 1742** on carta 150, then blank leaves, an **«END OF ITEM»** card at 203 and a resolution target at 205, and **resumes at 1743** in the next item. Interpolating across that join lands in the wrong decade.

**Both filmed parishes of the Contea di Pisino are now nil for the window** — Tinjan 1741–1749, Pazin 1740–1748. **And neither touches Kobler**, because Gologorica, Gračišće, Pićan and Žminj are in no part of this collection.

**This item is now an errand, not a read.** What would answer it is the **Državni arhiv u Pazinu**, which holds the books themselves. *Leave the item open; do not close it on these nils.*

---

**21 September 2026 — out of reach of full-text search, measured.** FamilySearch full-text indexes **Italian civil registration**, not the Croatia Church Books: 97 collections sampled from its own results carry **zero** Croatian entries. This item is a Croatian church register and **no query will reach it**. It stays an archive question.

---

**21 September 2026 — the premise is in doubt.** FamilySearch's own household index for **image 150** reads the 29 May 1748 baptism as **«Josephum Aloysium MANCOSCHI», parents «Joannis Bapte Mancoschi» and «Magdalená Mancoschi»** — the same date, the same child's forenames and the same parents' forenames this archive records as **Defranceschi**, with a different surname. Either the index misread *de Franceschi*, or this household was never ours and **there is no second Fiume house to relate Valentino's to**. **The plate has not been magnified** and until it is, this item cannot be answered — it can only be asked more precisely. See [/searched/](/searched/).

**21 September 2026, later — SETTLED, and the premise holds.** The plate reads *«Josephum Aloysium filium legitimum D.ni Joannis Baptæ et D.næ Magdalenæ jugalium **DE FRANCESCHI**, natus 28 hujus»*. **The index's «Mancoschi» is simply wrong.** There are two Defranceschi households at Fiume in the 1740s and the question of how they relate is live again. **The godparents are Josephus Voxila and Eleonora Frauel — neither a Defranceschi — so this entry does not itself join the two houses.** The next move is the same treatment on Valentino's sixteen baptisms, looking for a Defranceschi in anyone's godparent line.

**21 September 2026, third pass — the first of Valentino's baptisms read on the plate.** **17 September 1739**: *«Matthæus Franciscus filius legitimus **D. Valentini et Helenæ jugalium Defranceschi**… Patrini fuere **Nob. D.nus Petrus Ronaldi**, et **Nob. D.na Margarita uxor D.ni Georgij Vlah, Capitanei Cast[u]anensis**»*. **No Defranceschi godparent** — so this entry does not join the houses either, and that is now two baptisms read with the same negative.

**What it does give is the social register.** Valentino is styled ***D.*** in the very year he became a citizen of Fiume, and his son's godparents are **nobles**, one of them the wife of the **Captain of Kastav**. Joannes Baptista's household is likewise *D.ni* with *D.nus/D.na* godparents. **Two Defranceschi houses in one port, both addressed as gentry, in one decade** — a shared milieu, not yet a shared descent. **Next: the remaining baptisms of Valentino × Helena, same treatment.**

**21 September 2026, fourth pass — four baptisms read, and the negative is now solid.** 17 Sep 1739, 4 Sep 1741, 29 May 1748 and 26 Jun 1752, all read off the plate. **Not one Defranceschi among the eight godparents.** Every one of the eight carries an honorific — four are *Nobilis* — including the wife of the **Captain of Kastav** and the noble widow **Antonia Monaldi**, who stands for other families on the same leaf. **Both households move among the port's nobility; no thread yet joins them to each other.** *Vitipolis*, the index's place for Valentino's children, is very probably **Fiume** itself — *Terra Fluminis Sancti Viti*, the city of St Vitus — which removes the apparent contradiction with the film. *(inf.)*

**22 September 2026 — fifth baptism read, same answer.** 19 December 1742, *Francisca Joanna Theresia*, godparents **D. Antonius de Campo Xenes** and **Nob. D.na Vidua Margaritha Salopp**. **Five baptisms, ten godparents, no Defranceschi.** Also settled: *Mattio* and *Antonio*, held here as children born 1742 and 1753, are **burials** — so Valentino and Helena lost a child in July 1742 and an infant in September 1753. **The godparent route is close to exhausted; the marriage registers are the next place to look.**

**22 September 2026 — the marriage route tested and the index is empty.** Exact-surname *Franceschi* marriages across Croatia 1715–1775 return **120**, filtered to Fiume **62**, and **neither Fiume marriage is among them**. Most of the 62 are **Omiš**; two that looked like our couple are 1846 and 1852 **Masatto** marriages where *Franceschi* is a mother's maiden name; one genuine 1738 marriage (*Antonio × Margaritta Cambi*) sits on **film 005494172**, not Fiume's, with no place given.

**This item is not answerable from an index**, and that is now shown rather than supposed. The route is **the Fiume marriage register read on the plate**. **And the possibility that the answer is «they are not related» should stay open** — five baptisms with no Defranceschi godparent is the shape unrelated households make.

**22 September 2026 — the marriage register is open, and it was never a separate film.** The volume is **«Births 1734–1749 · Marriages 1734–1753», Rijeka** — one book, filmed as **005497925**, baptisms to about image 155 and **marriages in the back fifty frames**. This archive had been treating the film as a baptism register.

**Frame 175, 28 February 1740**: *«…in matrimonium conjunxit D.nus Canonicus Devicho, **præsentibus testibus D.no Valentino Defranceschi**, et D.no Gregorio Kesner»*. **Valentino stands witness at a Fiume wedding**, styled *D.no*, four months after becoming a citizen. The next entry on the same leaf is witnessed by **Nob. D. Antonio Spingarolli**, godfather to Valentino's son in 1741. **Defranceschi, Spingarolli and Monaldi recur together across both registers.**

**Still to read: the remaining fifty frames.** A marriage of either Fiume man would name his parents outright, which is the one thing that would settle this item either way.

---

**22 September 2026 — the front of the marriage volume is closed, and the «remaining fifty frames» line was stale.**

**Frames 160–167, both pages: 1 January 1734 to November 1736. No Defranceschi in any role** — not groom, bride or witness.

**The volume has a beginning, and this is it.** Frame **160 left** is a blank leaf; frame **160 right** carries the heading ***«Liber Matrimoniorum Anni 1734. Sit Laus Deo, ac B. Virgini Mariæ»*** on book page **150**, with the first entry dated **1 January 1734**. Frames **155–159** are the tail of the *baptism* volume, still in **1749** — the two registers sit back to back in one book, and the marriage section runs **160 → 1734** onward while the baptisms run to 1749, so the film's date order reverses at frame 160.

**What that settles:** Valentino's wedding of **28 February 1737** is the **first Defranceschi marriage in the book**, with nothing of the name before it. Read together with the 20 September sweep of **168–191**, the surname appears **once** in fourteen years of Fiume weddings, 1734–1748.

**And the reading of his own entry is corrected in one place.** The second witness, published here as *«Nob. D.no Antonio **Moretti**»*, is **Nob. D.no Antonio MONALDI** — magnified and set beside a securely-read *«Laurentius Monaldi»* two frames earlier in the same hand, where the looped **ld** ligature is identical and the double **t** of *Moretti* is simply not on the page. **So Valentino's own wedding is witnessed by a Monaldi**, on the day he married, in the parish the Monaldi archpriest ran — the earliest link in the **Defranceschi–Spingarolli–Monaldi** circle by two years. *(The archpriest **Petrus Maria Monaldi** died in the autumn of 1736; a marginal note on frame 167 records the parish vacant until 4 March 1737 and a new parish priest installed 29 September 1737, which is why a canon and not the archpriest marries Valentino.)*

**The bride's surname gains a third live reading.** The initial is this hand's ambiguous looped capital, so *Surcho* and *Zurcho* stand — but the body of the word is plainly **-urcho**, and **Turcho** belongs on the list beside them, because *Turco / Turcho* is a common name on this coast and *Surcho* is not. *Given as read; no one of the three is preferred.*

**Unread is not fifty frames, it is the tail.** **168–191 were read on 20 September**; the note above asking for «the remaining fifty frames» was written without that sweep in view. What is genuinely unread is **192 onward** — frame **200** is **1751**, and the volume's marriages end in **1753**. *That stretch is after Joannes Baptista's son was born, so it cannot hold his marriage; it is worth reading for any other Defranceschi, and for whether he appears as a witness.*

---

**22 September 2026, later — the Fiume marriage volume is read END TO END, and the count is one.**

**Frames 160–204. 1 January 1734 to 7 February 1753. Nineteen years, both pages of every frame.** Frame **204 right is a blank leaf** (book page 194) and frame **205 is the microfilm's «END OF ITEM» card**, so the volume has a documented back cover as well as a documented title page.

**In nineteen years of Fiume weddings the surname appears once: Valentino's, 28 February 1737.** Not as a groom, not as a bride, not as a witness — with the single exception already known, Valentino standing witness on 28 February 1740.

**The tail read today, 192–204, is Joannes Baptista's last chance and he is not in it either.** June 1748 to February 1753, the years *after* his son's birth. He does not marry at Fiume before 1748 and he does not marry at Fiume after it; his Fiume marriage is to **Catharina de Benzoni in 1771**, in volume 2, as a **widower**. *Magdalena was married somewhere else, and this volume can no longer be asked about her.*

**The join between the two sweeps was tested, not assumed.** Frame 191 ends on **25 February 1748** and frame 192 opens on **2 June 1748** — a three-month hole exactly where two sessions' work meets, which is the most dangerous place on a reel. **It is not a missing leaf.** The pencil foliation runs **181 → 182** unbroken across the two frames, and **Ash Wednesday 1748 fell on 28 February**: the last wedding is three days before Lent begins and the register resumes after it. *The gap is the closed season, and the book is whole.* [Logged as method](/method/).

**One caution on the Monaldi correction above.** *Moretti* is **not** absent from this volume — an *«Antonium filium Bartholomæi **Moretti** Forojuliensem ex Gradisca»* marries on **14 February 1753**, frame 204. The correction rests on the letterforms at native resolution and on the comparison with a securely-read *Monaldi*, **not** on the surname being impossible here. *Said plainly because a correction that leans on an absence which turns out not to exist is worse than the error it replaced.*

**And a caution on the circle.** *Defranceschi–Spingarolli–Monaldi* has been read here as a pattern around this family. On **2 February 1752** (frame 201) **Nob. D.no Petro Monaldi and Nob. D.no Antonio Spingarolli witness together** at the wedding of a daughter of **Nob. D.no Josephi de Franchi** — a different family. The same pair witnesses for **de Franchi** again on 9 July 1752. **Monaldi and Spingarolli are the port's standing noble witnesses**, not a tie peculiar to this name. *The 1737 Monaldi at Valentino's wedding is still worth having; it is evidence of standing, not of kinship.*

**What this item has left.** Fiume is exhausted for the marriage question: both the volume and the index have now been asked and answered. The item stands where it stood — **Magdalena's maiden name**, in the County of Pazin's own books at the **Državni arhiv u Pazinu**. *An errand, not a read.*

---

**22 September — a name in the right decade, and nothing more.** The Svetvinčenat sweep has turned up **a Joannes Baptista de Franceschi alive there on 19 April 1739**, and a second of that name dead before October 1737.

**This is not a lead yet and is not recorded as one.** Fiume's Joannes Baptista fathers a child in **1748** and his origin is unknown; Svetvinčenat is **sixty kilometres away** in Venetian Istria, not the Contea di Pisino that Kobler points at. *No document connects the two, and the same register has just shown that this family reuses forenames freely enough that a match on one proves nothing.*

**What would make it a lead:** the **Svetvinčenat marriages 1762–1858** or the parish's own earlier marriage book, if either names a Joannes Baptista leaving the parish — or a Fiume entry giving his birthplace. *(lore, and deliberately held at that.)*

---

**23 September 2026 — a Carnian Giovanni Battista, in Istria, six years early.**

**Svetvinčenat, 20 December 1742:** *«Patrini fuerunt **Joannes Baptista de Franceschi, ex Cargn.**, et Maria uxor Gasparis Perlar»* — **the only person of the name in that whole register given an origin**, because he was not of the parish. ***Cargna* is the Venetian form of *Carnia***.

**This is the phrase this item has been circling.** Fiume's marriage register puts *«ex Carnia»* on **Valentino** in 1737; Fiume's **Joannes Baptista** fathers a child in **1748** and his origin has never been found. **Here is a Joannes Baptista de Franceschi from Carnia, in Istria, in 1742.**

**It is not evidence that they are the same man and this item does not treat it as such** — *the register gives no age, no wife, no destination, and this family reuses forenames freely enough that a match on one proves nothing.* **What it changes is where to look.** The question was *«where did Fiume's Joannes Baptista come from»*, answered only by Kobler's assertion of the Contea di Pisino. *There is now a documented Carnian of that exact name forty kilometres away, six years before.*

**The next move is unchanged in kind and sharper in aim:** the Svetvinčenat marriage books that Pazin holds digitally for **1674–1762** — the stretch FamilySearch does not film — because a marriage entry would give this man a father and a home village.

---

**28 September — a second Fiume household falls out of yesterday's date corrections, and it is not the one this item is about.**

*Two rows whose dates had been copied from other people's burials turned out to sit on real Fiume baptisms: **Anna Maria, 4 March 1801**, and **Pietro, 10 April 1803**, the latter naming his mother **Ursula**. They were briefly and wrongly attached to **Valentino × Helena** — whose children stop in 1757.*

**They belong to Valentinus Defranceschi, born 1775/76, who married Ursulam De Berzoni at Fiume on 6 October 1793.** *The marriage act is `1:1:6YBR-ZFPR` and names the couple together, so it is now a spouse link in the roster rather than an assumption.*

**⚠ And it puts a name one letter away from this item's own open question.** *Item 143 has been waiting on **Magdalena's maiden name**, with Joannes Baptista's second marriage — to **Catharina de BENZONI**, 9 December 1771 — as the only Benzoni in view. Here is a **de BERZONI** marrying a Defranceschi at the same parish twenty-two years later.* **Benzoni and Berzoni may be one family or two, and nothing read so far decides it**: *the difference is a single letter in two clerks' hands, and this archive has already had one surname correction of exactly that kind this month — Moretti read for Monaldi on a looped ligature.* **Not treated as a lead. Recorded so that whoever opens the Pazin books knows to test both spellings.**

rows.what: The ÖStA catalogue, mined to the person — twenty on the roster and four files that would give a household
rows.note:
**Ninety-nine catalogue records, fifty of this name, twenty people now on the roster — and none of the files themselves has been opened.**

The catalogue gives rank, posting and sometimes birthplace for free. **Four of the fifty would give a household if ordered**, because of what the document type is rather than what the catalogue says:

· **`AT-OeStA/KA Marine NMA Pers OffBea Akten MGBBl 2651` — Johann Defranceschi, born 1833 at Gallignana.** A *Marinegrundbuchblatt* gives **birthplace, parents, religion, marriage and children**. For a man out of **Gračišće**, the origin parish, that is the single most valuable unopened document in this list.
· **`AVA Justiz JM Präs. A 134.22` — Carl Dragutin Defranceschi, born 29 July 1883 at Zara.** A *Prospetto dello stato personale* gives birthplace, parents and career.
· **`AVA Justiz JM Präs. A 140.14` — Giovanni Pietro de Franceschi, born at Rovigno.** A *Personalstandesausweis*, same shape.
· **`KA Marine NMA Pers VerEv KL-GagoRangkl 725` — Josef Franceschi, born at Almissa.** The first man here documented as *born* at **Omiš** by a state record.

**All four are public and permission-free**, so the cost is reproduction, not research — and the Kriegsarchiv's own EUR 45 *search* fee is [already shown to be unnecessary](/searched/) where the file is catalogued to the item.

**Ordered together they would test something this archive cannot otherwise test:** whether the Austrian service families of the name — Venice, Zadar, Omiš, Rovinj, Gračišće — are one stock or several. *Four documents, one envelope.*

**⚠ 28 September — the catalogue is unreachable, and this is the instrument failing rather than the archive.** * resolves to **85.158.227.121** and then **times out on port 443**. Tested from the same machine and the same minute in which FamilySearch connects normally, so it is not this network.* **The free field search that answered the €45 question on 20 September does not answer at all today.** *Nothing is concluded from the silence: a catalogue that will not open is not a catalogue that holds nothing, and this item keeps every record it already has. Retry before assuming anything has changed.*

rows.what: The living rule, applied to strangers as well as relatives — the rest of the site
rows.note:
**The roster has been tested against the dates. The other pages have not, and the answer is David's rather than this archive's.**

The rule as published is *«living relatives are named and nothing more»* — written for **family**, and applied by a hand-set flag that could only ever catch people David knew to name. On 22 September the roster was tested mechanically instead and **eight strangers born 1931–1946 with no death recorded** came out; they now print name and place only.

**The same test has not been run on the narrative pages, and they hold more.** On [the diaspora page](/diaspora/) alone:

· **The Philadelphia family of 1954** — *«Bosiljka Defranceski, born 1918, with **Brank born 1942**, **Jela born 1946** and **Mojuil born 1947**»*. Three people who would be in their late seventies and eighties.
· **Nelida Albina, born 9 September 1931 at Mercedes** — a full date, from an Argentine baptism ark.
· **Angelo born 17 May 1927 and Eugene born 5 September 1930** at Clarksburg, West Virginia.

**Every one of them is out of a public index**, and every one is somebody's private business if they are alive.

**The decision, plainly.** *Does the rule cover only the family, or everybody this site names?* If it covers everybody, the dates come out of those findings and the findings get thinner — the 1954 Philadelphia arrival is largely *made of* those dates. **This archive has not made that call and will not make it quietly**, because unlike every other question here it is not about accuracy. *The roster fix was done because the notice at its head made a claim that was untrue; extending it further changes what published research says, and that is David's to decide.*

---

**22 September 2026 — decided, by David, the same day it was put to him: the rule is about his relatives, as written.**

*«Family only.»* A person this site names from an **already-public index** keeps the dates that index publishes — **withholding them here makes nobody more private** and takes the substance out of the finding. The 1954 Philadelphia arrival, the Clarksburg brothers, the Dignano household in the refugee papers: **all keep their dates.**

**Three roster rows were put back the same hour.** Giordana, Maria and Claudio of the Dignano household had been held as possibly living for about ninety minutes; they came out of the **Arolsen collections**, not the family tree, so under the decision they keep what the file says. **Five rows stay held** — Nelida Albina, Feliciano, Richard, Assunta Maria and Daria — because those are **people in David's own tree**, and that is exactly who the rule is for.

**What survives from the exercise, and is worth more than the eight rows:** the test itself. *A hand-set flag cannot express «this person may be alive»* — it can only record who somebody remembered to mark. `living-audit.py` now runs the arithmetic first and prints anyone born within ninety-five years carrying neither a death nor a flag. **Today it prints none.** When the next import adds one, it will say so before anybody has to notice.

rows.what: 73 hosts the archive links to and never names in its bibliography
rows.note:
**`check:sources` is running on every build as of 22 September, and the first thing it says is that this archive cites seventy-three hosts it has never described.**

**Among them:** `cemla.com` (the Argentine arrival index), `collections.arolsen-archives.org` (which produced the Dignano household), `arhinet.arhiv.hr` (the Croatian state archives' catalogue), `archives.isula.corsica`, `archivesenligne.meurthe-et-moselle.fr`, `digitalna.nsk.hr`, `data.onb.ac.at`, `croatianroots.com`, `chan.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr`.

**Why it matters on a site whose whole argument is provenance.** [The bibliography](/sources/) is where this archive says **what a source is, what it gave, and where it is weak**. A host that appears only as a bare link in a table is a citation with no account of itself — *the reader is asked to trust a domain name.*

**The work is to write them up, not to delete the links**: each needs a line saying what the body is, what this archive got from it, and whether it is free, paywalled or behind a bot check. **Ten of the eighty-five already listed have no way to reach them at all** and say so, which is the standard the seventy-three should be brought to.

*The check reports and does not fail on this, so the number is a ratchet to drive down rather than a blocker.*

---

**Done, 27 September. `check:sources` no longer reports a single host.** *The count went **73 → 57 → 41 → 31 → 0** across four passes, and the bibliography went from 92 entries to **155**.*

**The material was mostly already written, and copying it would still have been wrong.** *Forty-six of the seventy-three hosts already had entries on [the research register](/searched/) saying what was asked and what came back.* **A generator turning those into «this archive has gone to it N times, see the register» would have passed the check and produced exactly what the item complains about** — *a citation with no account of itself.* **So they are written, one at a time.**

**Five of the seventy-three were never sources**, and giving them their own lines would have satisfied the check while misdescribing the archive. *`sg30p0.familysearch.org` is FamilySearch's own image server; `data.onb.ac.at` is ANNO's permalink host; and `artgallery.yale.edu`, `armchairgeneral.com` and `purl.org` appear only inside the **credit** field of a Wikimedia Commons image record — they are a licence's attribution chain, not bodies this archive consulted.* **Each now sits on the entry of the source it actually belongs to.** *Geneanet had two entries proposed and kept one: one body, one line.*

**What the pass turned up, beyond the writing.** *Žminj's own municipal history describes the «Carnielli» of Istria — men who spent part of each year back at **Agrons near Ovaro** and married only girls from there — which is the pattern this whole archive is trying to document, stated locally, and pointing at the same comune the Antenati survey reached independently.* **Udine's Notarile antico B. 2979, the protocols of Gio. Batta Franceschi, notary at Mione 1737–1783, is the best unread paper for the Carnic question and needs a letter rather than a search box.** *And the Museu da Imigração at São Paulo is not blocked but broken — every query returns HTTP 500 — so the Brazilian arrivals are unread rather than absent.*

rows.what: 36 groups of rows that may be one person recorded twice — and 57 that are certainly not
rows.note:
**Minting the frozen person ids on 23 September reported 48 collisions on name **and** birth **and** death, and this archive called them «probable duplicates» in writing without looking at one of them.** *Looked at on 27 September, that was wrong twice over: there are **33** groups, not 48, and **not one pair is identical** — every group differs in place, source or line.*

**Splitting them by PLACE separates the two halves cleanly.**

**17 groups / 41 rows sit in DIFFERENT parishes** — a Pietro of 1734 at Svetvinčenat, another at Bale, five more at Vodnjan; an Antonio of 1753 dead the same year at Rijeka, at Spalato and at Vodnjan. **These are not duplicates and must not be merged.** *A one-name study that did not produce them would be hiding something: the same saint's day, the same naming custom, the same decade, eight parishes.*

**16 groups / 34 rows share a name, dates AND place.** *Those are the candidates*, and the source pairs say why: **`burial` + `myheritage`**, **`household` + `read`**, **`grave` + `myheritage`**, **`household` + `myheritage`** — one person entered once from a record and once from the live tree is the classic shape. The list: Cristoforo 1824 Vodnjan (3), Domenico 1803 Vodnjan (3, all `read`), Bortolo 1756 Šterna, Leonardus 1766 Gologorica, Pietro and Domenica of Vodnjan, Franz 1822, Giovanni 1829 and Stefano 1831 Vodnjan, Julius 1833 Rijeka, Giovanni 1845 Ližnjan, Joanna 1848 Gologorica, Angelo 1851 Pola, Matteo 1874 Poreč, Giacomo at Broken Hill.

**Nothing has been merged.** *Each one is a judgement about two records and a person, not a string comparison, and the id minting deliberately froze both rows rather than guessing — a merge performed by a script is a person deleted by a script.* **Domenico of 1803 at Vodnjan is the one to start with: three rows, all from `read`, all one town.**

---

**Corrected within the hour, and the correction is bigger than the finding.** *The count above — 33 groups, 16 candidates — was produced by grouping on the **exact name string**. In an archive whose founding premise is that the name varies, that is the wrong key.*

**«Antonio De Franceschi» and «Antonio Defranceschi», both born 1704, both at Svetvinčenat, one from a record and one from the live tree, were two separate groups — because of one space.** They are the plainest duplicate signature in the file and the check walked past them.

**Folding the surname the way this archive's own `namefold` does** — stripping *de/di/del*, collapsing every spelling of the name to one token, dropping married names in brackets — gives:

· **93 groups, 228 rows** colliding on folded-name + birth + death
· **36 groups / 75 rows** share a **place** as well — the duplicate candidates
· **57 groups / 153 rows** are in different parishes — coincidence, and correct

**Twenty-six candidate groups were invisible to the exact-string check**, among them Mattia 1669, Zuana 1688, Batista 1692 and Antonio 1704 all at Svetvinčenat; a run of Vodnjan people from 1816 to 1833; and pairs where one row carries a married name in brackets — *Anna Defranceschi* and *Anna Defranceschi (Baichin)*, *Catarina* and *Catarina (Kisdaris)*, *Veneranda* and *Veneranda (Demarin)*.

*Still nothing merged. But the size of the job is twice what was published an hour ago, and the reason it was understated is the same fault as everything else this week: a check keyed on something other than the thing it was checking.*

---

**Adjudicated, 27 September — and the archive was already holding the proof.**

*Thirty-six groups share a folded name, a birth year, a death year and a place. The question was always which of them are one person written twice.* **The answer was in the `ark` field: where two rows carry the SAME FamilySearch ark, they are the same record entered twice, and that is proof rather than resemblance.** *Nothing had ever compared them.*

**Eighteen pairs are proven duplicates by identical ark** — *Mattia 1669, Zuana 1688, Batista 1692, Antonio 1704 and Maria Maddalena 1825 at Svetvinčenat; Domenica Maria 1816, Domenica Michiela Giovanna 1818, Stefano Matteo 1822, Pasqua 1825, Lucia 1826, Pietro 1828, Giovanni 1829 and Maria 1833 at Vodnjan; Pietro Antonio 1810 and Cattarina 1811 at Paluzza; Aloysius 1790 at Vižinada; Natale Mattio 1816; Franco at Rovinj.* **In every one, a register row and a MyHeritage row describe one child.**

**Seven pairs carry two DIFFERENT arks** and are not proven either way — *Mariam 1632, Bortolo 1756, Anna 1799, Elisabetta 1810, Gregorio 1822, Julius 1833, Giacomo d. 2012.* *Four of these pair a `6YBR`/`6YBT` ark against a `6B47` one, which looks like two collections indexing one event — but looking like it is not being it, and each needs the register.*

**Seven have an ark on one side only** and rest on circumstance: *Joannes Baptista 1752 and Joanna 1848 at Gologorica are identical in every field and are almost certainly a double insert; Marianna 1809 is the Mione child buried in the 1810 «Morti» at about a year old; Veneranda is the same wife of Antonio Demarin twice.*

**Ten pairs are distinct men and women whose rows say so in their own notes** — *the three Cristofori of Vodnjan, the Fiume shoemaker Giovanni q.m Pietro, the two Elene of Svetvinčenat, the two Giacomi, and the three Peters.* *These must never be merged, and the folded key would have merged them.*

*Full table: `data/duplicate-adjudication.json`.* **Nothing is merged yet.**

**The eighteen are merged, and not one address moved.**

*Deleting a duplicate row would delete a URL, and these pages have been published and linked since 23 September — which is the whole reason the person ids are frozen and never derived from a birth year.* **So the duplicate keeps its page and the page says what it is:** *a pointer to the person, with the ark that proves it.* **Everything the duplicate held was folded into the surviving row first** — *twenty fields, including every MyHeritage id, so nothing now exists only on the page that points away.*

**Which row survives is not a matter of taste.** *In all eighteen the pair is one register row against one MyHeritage row, and the register's spelling wins,* because this archive prefers what the document says to what a tree says about it. **No row of the direct line is touched.**

*`/person/` now lists **1,428** people rather than 1,446: it had been counting eighteen children twice.*

**⚠ One thing is left undone and is not mine to do.** *A `<link rel="canonical">` is what would stop a search engine indexing both addresses. `Base.astro` has no head slot and belongs to the session that owns the cross-site layout.* **The pointer is stated in prose, in the eyebrow and in the page description instead, and the head link should be added when that session next opens the layout.**

**The remaining seven need a register, and one attractive shortcut is dead.**

*Four of the seven pit a `6YBR`/`6YBT` ark against a `6B47` one, and it was tempting to read that as two FamilySearch collections indexing a single event — which would have settled all four at once.* **It is not true.** *Across the whole roster `6B47` runs to 123 arks and `6YBR` to 51, and both span several parishes and every kind of source: `6B47` is mostly Vodnjan but holds twelve Rijeka records, `6YBR` is mostly Rijeka.* **The prefix is ark hash space, not a collection, and it carries no information about what indexed the record.**

*The two arks must therefore be opened and compared. `curl` gets **403** from FamilySearch — the same client-filtering signature Antenati gives — and the API gives **401**. The browser session is signed out: every `ark:/61903/` URL redirects to the FamilySearch front page.* **Blocked until David signs in again**, at which point the seven are half an hour's work.

---

**And four LIVING women are each on the roster twice, which is two more than this archive thought.**

*Raised by the «Family research landing site» session on 27 September as a counting question, and the count led somewhere else.* **`check:living` reports 54 and the roster carries 58 `living: true` rows** — *not a leak, and not a gate failure: the harvest keys by NORMALISED name, and `norm` strips a married surname in parentheses, so four pairs collapse to four keys.* **Both spellings stay protected**, because the bare form is a substring of the parenthetical one.

**What the collision exposes is the duplication underneath it.** *Each of the four is one woman entered twice from MyHeritage — once under her married name with no place, once with a place and no married name:* **Petrica Defranceski (Baviello) / Petrica Defranceski of Horsham; Lidija Defranceski (Ruffini) / Lidija Defranceski of Crikvenica; Renata Defranceski (Buck) / Renata Defranceski of Metzingen; Ursula Defranceski (Korn) / Ursula Defranceski of Urach.**

*Ursula and Renate were already known and already waiting on David. **Petrica and Lidija are new.*** **Nothing is merged and nothing will be without him:** *the ark test that settled the eighteen dead cannot be run here — these rows have no ark — and merging two records of a living relative on a resemblance is not a thing to do unasked.*

---

**Closed, 27 September. All seven remaining pairs opened on FamilySearch, and they split four to three.**

**Three are one person recorded twice:**

· ***Bortolo* — burial 1812 aged 56, son of **Gio Battista**, against a marriage of 1777 to **Zanetta Granisi**, son of **Gio Batta**. Same father; a man who marries at twenty-one is fifty-six in 1812.**
· ***Gregorio* — baptism at Ližnjan 1822, son of **Mattio** and **Madalena Peuc…**, against a marriage of 1845 **aged 23** to **Agata Schiffich**. 1845 less 23 is 1822.**
· ***Mariam* — the same baptism, **9 September 1632 at Rijeka**, indexed twice under two collections: «Delnice Deanery» and «Croatia, Church Books».**

**⚠ That last one is the limit of the ark test and is worth stating.** *This archive's rule since this morning has been that **two different arks prove two different records**. Mariam has two arks and one baptism, because **two FamilySearch collections overlap on the same parish**. The rule holds one way and not the other: **the same ark proves one record; different arks do not prove two.***

**Four are different people, and the parents settled every one:**

· ***Elisabetta*** — *a burial of 26 September 1810, father **Franco**, against a baptism of 2 April 1810, parents **Anna and Andrea**. **Two infants of one name, in one town, in one year, to two households.***
· ***Julius*** — *a burial of 25 August 1833 **aged 0**, against **Julius the father** naming a daughter in 1829.*
· ***Anna*** — *an infant buried in 1800, against **Anna the mother** at her daughter's baptism at Kaštelir in 1849.*
· ***Giacomo of Broken Hill*** — *a Find a Grave entry, **died 19 November 2012**, against the 1909 baptism of **Germano Defranceschi at Cloz, Trento**, which is a different man in a different country.*

**Two marriages fell out as spouses**, each from a record naming the couple together: *Bortolo × **Zanetta Granisi** (1777) and Gregorio × **Agata Schiffich** (1845).* **The roster now carries ten spouses, eight of them from documents rather than from the family chart.**

rows.what: Audited every value this archive feeds the shared Evidence component, against the kit's new Ungraded default
rows.note:
The landing-site session shipped kit **a35acb9**: `no` and `open` are out of the Evidence alias table, and an unrecognised level now renders **«Ungraded»** instead of resolving to «Family». *That changes published text wherever an archive was feeding it a value it did not recognise, so every feed here was checked rather than assumed.*

**Four feeds, and all four are clean.** *`l.status` on the lines page takes documented, inferred and lore. `p.confidence` on the people pages takes documented, inferred and lore. `d.conf` in the destinations table takes doc, inf and lore. `n.conn` took `no` six times — and no longer reaches the component at all, since it renders «No link shown».* **Nothing in this archive would come out as «Ungraded», and the kit can be updated without changing a word on any page.**

**The audit found a trap of this archive's own making, which is the part worth keeping.** *The destinations table mapped `conf` with a ternary: doc → documented, inf → inferred, **anything else → lore**, and lore renders as «Family».* **The `conf` field across this archive's data also takes `neg`, `strong` and `living`** — *and `neg` is the archive saying a thing is **not** this family.* **A negative finding would have been published under a badge reading «Family».** *No destination carries those values today, so nothing was wrong on the page; it was wrong in the same way the notables column was wrong before anyone looked.* **The mapping is now total and an unrecognised value renders «Ungraded» rather than the most credulous answer in the set.**

*Still outstanding: the kit here is **1.0.0** and updating it touches `site/package*.json`, which is shared ground. **David's call, or the kit owner's.** Until then the new living summary line — which states rows and names separately instead of printing either as «people» — will not appear in this build.*

rows.what: Split the overloaded `conf` field — it is a grade, a negation and a person marker under one key
rows.note:
**`conf` means three things in this archive's data and that is why the credulous defaults were dangerous.** *A grade of a claim in `families.json` and `explorer.json` (doc, inf, lore, probable, strong); a **negative finding** in `gists.json` (`neg` — «nothing yet joins the Gologorica house to the Gallignana line»); a **living person** in `ancestors.json` (`living`).*

**Every renderer that touches it has to guess which meaning it has**, and three of them guessed in the credulous direction before this was noticed. *The fallbacks are now loud and neutral, which is the right answer while the field is ambiguous — but it is a patch on the symptom.*

**The fix is to split the key:** *`grade` for the five evidence levels, and separate fields for a negation and for living status, which are not grades and should never reach a grading component.* *Not started. It touches four data files and five pages, and the loud defaults make it safe to do slowly.*

---

**28 September 2026 — measured instead of remembered, and it is four times the size this item claimed.**

*This item said «four data files and five pages». **It is seventeen files and 176 values**, and the shape of the problem is worse than «one key, three meanings». Counted by `scripts/audit-conf.py`, which exists so the next attempt starts from the real number and can re-check it in a second.*

| | |
|---|---|
| files carrying the field | **17** |
| values in total | **176** |
| key names | **`conf` ×147 and `confidence` ×29** — the same idea under two names |
| canonical grades (`doc`/`inf`/`lore`) | 110 |
| **the same grades spelled out** (`documented`/`inferred`) | **21** |
| a **second vocabulary** (`probable`/`strong`/`family`) | 25 |
| **free prose in the grade key** | 15 |
| **not grades at all** | **5** |

**The five that are not grades:** *`neg` ×2 in `gists.json` — a **negative finding**; `living` ×3 in `ancestors.json` **and `directline.json`** — a **person marker**.* **This item said `living` was in one file. It is in two.**

**⚠ And two failure modes this item had not named.**

· **`doc` and `documented` are the same grade written two ways**, as are `inf` and `inferred`. *A lookup table keyed on one **silently falls through** on the other — which is exactly the mechanism that produced the credulous defaults. The bug was never really about `neg` and `living`; it was about a key whose vocabulary nobody could enumerate.*
· **Fifteen values are sentences, not grades** — in `cheryl.json`, `diaspora.json`, `omis.json` and `rivers.json`. *A renderer that grades them will grade a paragraph.*

**Not started, and deliberately not started today.** *A rename touching seventeen data files and every renderer that reads them is not a thing to half-do at the end of a long session — **a partly-renamed key is worse than an overloaded one**, because the fallbacks that currently shout «Ungraded» would start shouting it at correctly-graded rows. The loud neutral defaults hold the line meanwhile.*

**What the split should be, now that the vocabulary is known:** *`grade` for the evidence levels, normalised to **one** spelling; `negative: true` for the two findings in `gists.json`; `living: true` for the three person markers; and the prose moved to a field that is plainly prose.* **The `probable`/`strong` scale in `explorer.json` and `lineages.json` is a separate decision** — *it is a different question being graded, and merging it into the doc/inf/lore scale would flatten a distinction rather than fix one.*

rows.what: Declare the decisions — the kit pin, the living policy, and 1,446 frozen person ids
rows.note:
**`data/decisions.json` holds the values that must not change quietly, and the gate refuses when one does.** *Not counts — `check-witness.py` does counts and only reports. These are judgements, and changing one should cost a deliberate edit in the same commit.*

**The pids are the reason this exists.** *A person id is minted once and never derived, because a derived id moves when a birth year is corrected and a moved id is a dead URL. The witness counts 1,446 of them and that number is identical whether or not one now addresses a different person — **a count cannot see a substitution**.* *The mapping is declared instead: adding is free, changing or removing refuses and names the person.*

*Also declared: the **kit pin**, and the **living policy** `named-bare` — which every other check reads rather than decides, so weakening it would widen what may publish while every gate still passed.* **All five refusals were provoked deliberately before the check was wired in.**

rows.what: The kit is ten commits behind, and the update is dry-run clean — David's call
rows.note:
**This archive pins the shared kit at `7210356` (26 September, 22:35) and ten commits sit ahead of it.** *Seven touch `checkliving.py`, two `checkkin.py`, one `Evidence.astro`, and two add new tools.* **Updating touches `site/package.json` and the lock, which is shared ground, so it is not this session's to do.**

**It was dry-run against this archive rather than argued about**: the kit at `31f7a5c` was cloned to a scratch directory and every kit check in the build was run against this site. **All pass.** *The single failure — `check:kit` on a missing `sitemap.xml` — reproduces identically on the CURRENT kit and is an artefact of a bare `astro build`, not of the update.*

**The reason to do it is `checkkin`, and the finding is true today whether or not the pin ever moves.** *The current gate prints «1446 people · 0 impossible relationship(s)».* **The new one prints «427 of 1446 people carry both dates and were examined · 546 a birth only, 54 a death only, 419 no year at all».** *This gate has been green over 1,446 people while examining **427 of them — thirty per cent** — and the line it printed did not say so.* **419 people in this archive carry no year at all and no build has ever mentioned it.**

*`checkliving` also gets more honest: «no living person reaches the build» becomes the row-and-name breakdown — **«59 flagged row(s) … under 55 distinct name(s) — 4 row(s) collapse»** — which is exactly what `scripts/check-witness.py` computes independently, and the two agree.* **The four collapsing rows are Petrica, Lidija, Renata and Ursula**, who would become visible in build output rather than only here.

**⚠ Expect the gate to REFUSE on the first build after the bump**, and that is the design: *`data/decisions.json` declares the pin, so moving it stops the build until it is re-declared in the same commit.* *A `site/.kitpin` will also appear untracked on the first build; it is meant to be committed.*

rows.what: Dates copied on a name match — eight withdrawn, seventeen still to check
rows.note:
**Found while opening the seven unresolved duplicate pairs on FamilySearch, and it is worse than the duplicates were.** *Twenty-five roster rows carry `yfrom: «a dated entry already in this project's own burials/graves/gologorica-line/households data»` — meaning the year was **not read from that person's record**. It was copied from another entry in this archive that shared the name.*

**Nine were opened. Eight are wrong.**

· *Five women called **Maria Defranceschi** — Browachio, Buman, Contossich, Covaz, Dobrez — all carried **b. 1757, d. 1757 at Rijeka**, from one burial. **Five women cannot each be born, die and acquire a married surname in the same year.** Browachio's own record is the birth of her daughter at **Termeno, Bolzano, in 1907**; Contossich's is her **marriage in 1788**; Dobrez's is her daughter's baptism at **Kaštelir in 1853**.*
· ***Maria (Covaz)** may not be a Defranceschi at all: her record is the baptism of **Mariam Covaz** in 1766, both parents Covaz, and the name does not appear in it.*
· ***Anna (Baichin)** was published as an infant dead in 1800. Her record is her daughter's baptism at Kaštelir in **1849**.*
· ***Julius* was published as born in 1833. His record is his daughter's baptism in **1829** — he was a father four years before his printed birth.*
· ***Giacomo d. 2012 of Broken Hill*** *sits on a record for **Germano Defranceschi, baptised at Cloz, Trento, in 1909**.*

**Eight rows have had their years withdrawn** and each now states what its record actually says. *Two — Covaz and Giacomo — are held pending a decision on whether the row should exist at all.* **`elisabetta-defranceschi-1810-2` was checked and stands**: *its baptism of 2 April 1810 at Fiume is consistent with the burial later that year, so that pair is a genuine duplicate candidate.*

**Seventeen rows of the twenty-five are still unchecked.** *Ten of them have no ark, so they cannot be settled this way at all.*

*The general fault: **a year copied because two rows share a name is not evidence, and this archive printed it as though it were.***

---

**Closed, 27 September. All twenty-five adjudicated, and the mechanism failed almost every time it could be tested.**

**Sixteen rows carried a record identifier that could be opened. Fifteen were wrong.** *The sixteenth — Matteo of Poreč — is **restricted by FamilySearch** («this record can only be displayed on certain accounts»), so it cannot be tested from here and its years are withdrawn rather than left standing on an untestable basis.*

**The shapes the error took:**

· ***A different person entirely.*** *Giuseppe «1784–1819» sits on **Teresa Defranceschi, born 1881 at Rivolta d'Adda, Cremona** — a woman, ninety-seven years later, five hundred kilometres away. Franciscus «1819–1892» sits on **Emanuel Antonius, baptised at Kaštelir on New Year's Day 1860**. Giovanni «1845–1846» sits on **Giuseppe Costante, born 1856 at Telve, Trento**.*
· ***The right person at the wrong century.*** *Anna Maria is genuinely a Defranceschi baptised at Fiume — **in 1801, not 1844**. Pietro is genuinely a Defranceschi baptised at Fiume — **in 1803, not 1884**.*
· ***Another child's dates, betrayed by the parish.*** *The Gologorica Joannes wore the years of a Joannes buried at **Ližnjan**; the Gologorica Josephus wore the years of a Josephus buried at **Kaštelir**.*
· ***An event of the wrong kind.*** *Francesco «d. 1686 at Pola» sits on a **baptism at Omiš in 1657**.*

**Four were not errors at all but double inserts** — *Joannes Baptista 1752, Joanna 1848, Leonardus 1766 and Joseph 1929, each entered twice from one reading.* **They are merged rather than stripped**, because a copied year can mean «this is the same person» as well as «this is the wrong person», and the two need opposite treatments.

**⚠ And two of the errors are worth more than the correction.** *Anna Maria (1801) and Pietro (1803) are both baptised at **Fiume** to a father called **Valentino** — and Pietro's act names his mother **Ursula**. That is two more children and a wife for the **Valentino of Fiume** whose household [item 143](/worklist/) exists to reconstruct.* **A wrong date led to a right record.**

**⚠ 28 September — a correction to the paragraph above, made the day after writing it.**

*Yesterday's closing note said Anna Maria (1801) and Pietro (1803) were **«two more children and a wife for the Valentino of Fiume whose household item 143 exists to reconstruct»**. **They are not.** Valentino × Helena's children run **1737–1757**, and Pietro's act names his mother **Ursula**, not Helena.*

**They belong to a later Valentino**: *Valentinus Defranceschi, born 1775/76, who married **Ursula de Berzoni at Fiume on 6 October 1793** — `1:1:6YBR-ZFPR`, an act that names the couple together.* **Right family, right port, wrong generation by two.**

*The irony is exact and is left standing: the sentence was written inside a commit whose whole subject was **«the right person at the wrong century»**, describing that error in other people's work while committing it.* **A vocabulary for a mistake is not protection against it.**

rows.what: Coverage, measured at last: this archive holds about 8% of the name on FamilySearch and has no spouse field
rows.note:
**Asked on 27 September whether every Defranceschi and every spouse had been harvested. The honest answer is no, and now there are numbers instead of an impression.**

**What the two subscription sources actually hold, counted signed-in on 27 September:**

· **FamilySearch, exact «Defranceschi» — 8,235 records.** *«De Franceschi» returns the same 8,235, so the index is insensitive to the space and the two are one bucket, not two.*
· **FamilySearch, «Defranceski» — 131.**
· **FamilySearch, «Franceschi» — 44,024**, *which is a broader name and mostly other families; this archive's one-name-study scope governs how much of it is in scope.*
· **Findmypast, exact «Defranceschi» — 548**: *113 birth, marriage, death and parish · 94 census, land and surveys · 328 travel and migration · 7 directories · 5 military · 1 education.*

**What this archive holds against that: 637 of its 1,446 rows carry a FamilySearch ark at all** — *and those 637 are spread across every spelling and every collection.* **Against the 8,235 Defranceschi bucket alone that is roughly eight per cent**, and no pass has ever gone through that result set methodically. *What exists instead is a set of targeted searches, each written up on [the research register](/searched/), which is a different thing from a harvest.*

**⚠ And spouses are not harvested at all.** *The roster has **no spouse field** — the word does not appear in its schema.* *Spouses exist only in `households.json` (**132** entries) and in the eight generations of `directline.json`.* **Of 1,339 people in the dossiers, none carries a spouse.** *So a marriage in the index — which is frequently the only record naming a woman's maiden family — has nowhere to go in this archive's main table.*

*The work this implies is a harvest rather than a search: page the 8,235, take the ark, the event, the place and every named relation, and reconcile against the 637 already held. **The 548 on Findmypast are the smaller and more urgent half, because that subscription ends about 16 October.***

rows.what: Findmypast harvested whole: all 548 records of the name, in `data/harvest/`
rows.note:
**The first complete harvest this archive has ever taken from a subscription source.** *Not a targeted search — **every** record Findmypast holds under the exact surname, paged end to end: 28 pages, **548 records, 548 distinct ids, no gaps and no duplicates**, matching the site's own reported total exactly.*

**How, so it can be repeated before the subscription ends about 16 October.** *The results page is a React app over a GraphQL API whose root query is not reachable by hand and whose introspection is switched off. The records are in the page's own Apollo cache, `window.__APOLLO_CLIENT__.cache.extract()`, keyed `Record:`. Paging is the parameter **`_page`**, not `page` — `page` silently returns a zero-result search rather than an error. Each page was read into `sessionStorage`, which survives same-origin navigation, and dumped once at the end.* **No bot check was met and none was circumvented.**

**What the 548 are.** *By category: **301 passenger-list entries**, 66 census, 54 civil deaths, 39 marriages and divorces, 28 electoral-roll, 15 migration, 12 naturalisations, 16 parish records, 7 directories, 5 First World War draft cards, 1 school pupil.* *By place: 260 «Americas» and 196 United States, **46 Australia**, 32 England, 12 Italy, and one each in Wales and **Smyrna**.* *Years run **1842 to 2023**, with 25 records carrying none; the peak is the 1910s (83) and the 1930s (71).*

**The index spells the name two ways and they are not interchangeable**: *366 as «de Franceschi», 173 as «Defranceschi», plus a «De-Franceschi» and a «Guglielmetti Defranceschi». Seven records carry **no forename at all** and seven more are directory pages with no person on them.*

**⚠ Nothing is reconciled yet, and most of it is not this family.** *These are index rows — id, forename, surname, year, record set, place. The transcripts behind them are a separate fetch and the images another. **No row has been matched against the roster and none should be assumed to be a relative:** the Memphis, Chicago, Detroit, Torrington and Puerto Rico clusters are visibly other households.* *The next step is reconciliation against the 637 arks already held, then the transcripts — while the subscription lasts.*

---

**The harvest was incomplete and the archive's own notes caught it.** *`findmypast.json`, written 16 September, records the corpus by spelling: **«defranceschi» 548** — which the harvest matched exactly, eleven days later, so the corpus is stable and the paging sound — but also **«defranceski» 36, «different, and almost entirely this family»**.* **That spelling had not been harvested.** *It is now: `data/harvest/findmypast-defranceski.tsv`, 36 records, matching the recorded figure.*

**And it is the family, unlike most of the 548.** *Zdravko and Ruža at Horsham; Tobias's 1922 passport; the Memphis household of 1910 — Antonio, Bertha, Pietro, Alberts, Aurora, Alba, six people on consecutive lines; a Detroit household of 1930 — Domme, Augusta, Ann, Irene, John, Joseph, six more.*

**⚠ Two probate files, and this archive did not know they existed.** *`AU/VICTORIA/WILLSPROBATE/000697550` — **Zdrovko de Franceski, Victoria, 1980**. `AU/VICTORIA/WILLSPROBATE/001185884` — **Rosa Defranceski, Victoria, 1996**.* **A probate file names heirs**, which is precisely what the Australian branch is missing, and it is a different document from the death registration already sought on item 68.

**A date that looks like a contradiction and is not.** *Findmypast gives Zdravko's Victorian civil death as **1980** and the probate as **1980**; this archive has him dying **22 December 1979 at Horsham**, documented, and the BillionGraves index agrees at 1979.* **A death eight days before the new year is registered and probated in the following one.** *The 1979 stands; the 1980 is the registration year and is recorded here so that nobody later «corrects» a right date with it.*

**One lead nobody has followed.** *Five people land in Pennsylvania in **1954** under this spelling — **Bosiljka, Branko, Jela, Josip and Mojuil Defranceski** — Croatian given names, arriving together, five years after the Australian party of 1949. **No US arrival of this family in the 1950s is anywhere in this archive.***

rows.what: Trove, harvested whole with an API key — and a Broken Hill household nobody had
rows.note:
**170 distinct newspaper and gazette articles, every spelling, saved to `data/harvest/trove-newspapers.json`.** *Held back until now by a wrong assumption: that Trove folds the space in «De Franceschi» the way FamilySearch and Findmypast do. **It does not** — 13 articles fused, 128 spaced, **three in common** — so the earlier passes had swept a tenth of the source and called it done.*

**Five people with addresses and exact dates, out of the Commonwealth Gazette's naturalisation notices, all free:**

· **Cesare De Franceschi** — naturalised **28 January 1963**, of **497 Wyman Lane, Broken Hill**.
· **Anna Maria De Franceschi** — naturalised **28 August 1966**, of **the same 497 Wyman Lane**. *A household, three years apart; the gazette does not say whether wife or daughter.*
· **Bernardino De Franceschi** — naturalised **26 September 1964**, of **350 Piper Street, Broken Hill** — a second address of the name in the same town.
· **Albino De Franceschi** — naturalised **27 February 1969**, of **25 Edgevale Road, Bulleen, Victoria**.
· **Gabriella De Franceschi** — **executrix of the will of Mario Bazzacco**, who died 12 June 1973, NSW Probate Division notice of 29 March 1974.

**Broken Hill was already on this archive's map** — *[Giacomo Defranceschi](/person/giacomo-defranceschi-d2012/) is buried there* — *and it now has two documented addresses and three named people in the 1960s.* **No connection to this family is shown for any of them and none is claimed.**

*Still to do: the 12 Canberra Times «Family Notices» of 1977–1994, the 1954 Alice Springs drowning reported in three papers, and the non-newspaper categories — **176 books** under «De Franceschi» that no pass has opened.*

---

**The twelve «Family Notices» are read, and they put a family on a pin that had nobody on it.**

**«The Canberra Times», 25 September 1982:** *«**DE FRANCESCHI, Cesira.** — Sept 23, **Pederobba, Italy**. Dearly beloved mother of **Cesare, Canberra**, **Giosue Giacomo and Dino, Broken Hill**, **Alfonso, Mario and Imelda, Italy**. Loved grandmother of their children.»* A mass followed at **St Thomas Aquinas, Charnwood** on 2 October.

**Two things this archive already held, and never joined.** ***Pederobba, in Treviso**, is a pin on David's own emigration map — one of the Veneto places marked «High Level of Emigration from Here» — and it had **no person attached to it**. And **[Giacomo Defranceschi](/person/giacomo-defranceschi-d2012/)** was a name on a stone in Broken Hill Cemetery with no origin, no parents and no siblings.* **One death notice supplies both: the Broken Hill Defranceschi are a Pederobba household, and three brothers of them went to the same mining town.**

*It also explains the gazettes: **Cesare De Franceschi**, naturalised at **497 Wyman Lane, Broken Hill** in 1963 and living at Canberra by 1982, is the Cesare of the notice; **Anna Maria**, naturalised from the same address in 1966, is the Anna who appears beside him in notices for the next thirty years.*

**⚠ What is NOT published, and needs David's decision.** *The remaining notices — engagements, marriages, births and birthdays from 1977 to 1994 — name **three generations of living people**: Cesare and Anna's children and their children, with years of birth derivable from «Happy 21st» and «Happy 25th» notices, and their suburbs.* **None of it is on the site.** *The 22 September rule says the living rule is family only and that strangers in public indexes keep their dates — but these are living private individuals in Canberra with no shown connection to this family, and compiling a household of them from birthday notices is a different act from recording a naturalisation.* **Held entirely, pending a decision.**

**The 62 pre-1940 articles are read, and 35 of them are one dead painter.** *Every «Advertising» hit from 1879 to 1921 is an auction catalogue listing **«M. DE FRANCESCHI»** among a column of painters — **Mariano de Franceschi, b. 1849**, who is already on this archive's notables page. The name is in the Melbourne papers for forty years and the man was never in Australia.*

**Ten real people were under them**, now on the roster with no dates, because a newspaper names without ageing: *a **Franceski household at Lismore** (Dr C. Franceski; a Miss Franceski; **Amelia**, the music teacher who became Mrs Sullivan; **Caesar** of North Lismore, persimmons and olives at the 1934 Sydney Royal Show); **G. Franceski** racing bicycles at Beverley, WA; **Annie Amanda Franceski Kean**, divorced at Maryborough in 1901; and **Rev. Joseph de Franceschi, C.M.**, a Vincentian at Rio in 1912 and Regional Director for Brazil in 1930 — **the first named person of this name this archive has found in Brazil**, where its own map has marked a cluster for months with nobody on it.*

rows.what: The Trove key was issued on a written undertaking this archive has been breaching
rows.note:
**Raised by the D'Arcy session on 27 September, verified here, and correct.** *The letter is real: `notes/letters/2026-09-17-trove-api-RSref189042.md` in the D'Arcy archive, **sent to Trove Support on 20 September 2026, unchanged, at David's instruction**. It answers the Library's question about AI use, and it is why the key exists.*

**What David undertook**, in his own words: *«**No full text of any article would be retrieved. The request is metadata only** — newspaper and gazette titles, their place coverage and their date ranges»*, and that the archive *«would cite Trove as the source of a **title and a date range and nothing more**»*.

**What this archive did on 27 September, before anyone had read the letter:**

· **Searched articles, not titles.** *The undertaking describes the two titles endpoints; this used `/v3/result` against article records. **That is outside the stated scope even when nothing textual comes back.***
· **Published 53 article snippets** — *7,898 characters of newspaper prose — to `data/harvest/trove-newspapers.json`, tracked, committed in `c164d56` and pushed to a public remote.* **Removed from the file the same day**; *the field is gone and the reason is recorded in the file itself.*
· **Fetched the full text of about seventy articles** from `nla.gov.au` to read the naturalisation notices and family notices. *Not through the API, but «no full text of any article would be retrieved» does not turn on which door it came through.*
· **Quoted six passages of article prose into the published site data**, including the Cesira De Franceschi death notice that is the best single finding of the day.

**⚠ Two things are NOT done and are David's, not this session's.**

1. ***The snippets remain in git history.*** *Removing them from `HEAD` does not remove them from `c164d56`, and the remote is public. Rewriting published history is destructive for anyone who has cloned, so it waits on him.*
2. ***The six quoted passages are still published.*** *Whether citing a 1982 death notice by paper, date and page — and quoting the sentence that names seven children — is «a title and a date range and nothing more» is a question about a commitment David made. **This session will not answer it by deleting the finding, and will not answer it by keeping it either.***

**No further Trove article search or article-text fetching until David decides.** *The D'Arcy session's suggestion is the right one: the Library answered four questions in ten days and was not difficult, so if the archives want article search, that is a short note asking for it rather than a quiet widening — and better than having the key pulled from all seven archives at once.*

**27 September, later — D'Arcy checked their own archive against this and found the same fault there.** *Twenty-seven article-level Trove references: twenty-five are links inside their raw MyHeritage export, other people's tree notes from 2017 and never retrieved by them — but **two are in a file that archive writes**, and one quotes six words of an 1849 obituary. Pre-key, from the website, not the API, and by the argument this archive accepted, that does not turn on which door it came through.* **Both archives are now in front of David with the same question.**

*They will draft the letter, and their framing is right and is adopted here: **it has to be a disclosure, not a request.** «May we also search articles» omits that the searching already happened, and the Library would discover that the moment it looked at either repository. **Better from us than from them.** The draft goes to David and nothing is sent without him.*

**No Trove call of any kind is made from this archive until David answers — including the titles endpoints, which are the sanctioned use.** *Not because titles are in doubt, but because the posture while a breach is on the table is to stop, not to find the part that is still allowed.*

**The figure going into the letter was re-verified, and the first version of it was unsound.** *D'Arcy asked to use the space-folding result as the answer to «why do you want article search». The overlap of **3** had been measured by comparing the 13 fused ids against **the first 100 of 128** spaced ids — a hundred of a hundred and twenty-eight, quoted as though it covered them all. The true figure could have been anything from 3 to 13.* **It holds:** *«De Franceschi» returned 128 and contributed **125 records not already seen**, so exactly three were already held, and the id-level test places all three in the fused set.* **Two derivations, one answer.**

*A stronger statement of the same fact, also verified: across the five spellings this family uses, Trove returns **180 hits and 170 distinct records** — **only ten records in the whole set are reachable by more than one spelling.** These are not one corpus seen five ways; they are five nearly disjoint corpora, and a researcher who searches the spelling their own family happens to use sees a fraction of what is there.*

**The letter names the two archives separately rather than averaging them**, which is D'Arcy's call and the right one: *a paragraph that blends a bulk machine retrieval with a six-word phrase from a person record invites the reader to assume the worse of both.* *It is at `notes/letters/2026-09-27-trove-disclosure-RSref189042.md` in their repository, with the do-nothing-and-narrow alternative beside it, and goes nowhere without David.*

**⚠ 29 September 2026 — David: «not sending letters yet.» This item waits on that decision and is not to be raised again until he lifts it.** *Recorded once, here, so no session re-opens it by suggesting the letter afresh.*

---

**⚠ 29 September 2026 — David has answered the second question: «keep the six quoted passages published.»**

*This archive [put the question to him and declined to answer it either way](/worklist/) — «this session will not answer it by deleting the finding, and will not answer it by keeping it either». **He has answered it. The six passages stay.*** *Among them the **Cesira De Franceschi death notice**, the best single finding of that day, and the sentence in it that names seven children.*

**Recorded as his decision, because it is one.** *The undertaking to the National Library was given in his name and in his words; whether a 1982 death notice cited by paper, date and page falls inside «a title and a date range and nothing more» is his call to make and he has made it.* **No session is to re-open it or quietly narrow the quoting on its own initiative.**

**⚠ ONE QUESTION REMAINS OPEN, and it is the other one.** *The **53 article snippets are still in git history** — 7,898 characters, in commit `c164d56`, on a public remote. Removing them from `HEAD` did not remove them from the commit. **That is untouched and undecided**, and it is destructive to fix, so it waits on him.*

**And nothing is sent.** *Per [the standing instruction of the same day](/worklist/), the disclosure letter stays drafted and held.*

rows.what: A pier in Rijeka carries the name, and nobody has said which man it honours
rows.note:
**There is a pier in the port of Rijeka called «De Francescijev gat», and this archive does not know who he was.**

**What it is.** *[Arca Adriatica](https://arcaadriatica.eu/?pr=i&id=13548), entry **13548** — «**Pristanište Zichy / De Francescijev gat**», «Pier Zichy / Pier de Franceschy».* **A stone-block pier in the Rijeka port basin**, between the **Istrian pier** to the east and the **Vienna pier** to the west: *east face **150 m**, west face **134 m**, south face **80 m**, about **6 m** alongside, with stairs down to the water and rail-mounted cranes — a 300 kN heavy-lift on the east side, two 30 kN mobile cranes on the west.* **It is working port infrastructure, not a monument.**

**What the source is.** *Arca Adriatica is a **virtual museum of Adriatic maritime heritage** built under an EU Interreg Italy–Croatia project — Primorje-Gorski Kotar County, Malinska-Dubašnica, the Kvarner County Tourist Board, the House of Batana at Rovinj, Cervia, Cesenatico, San Benedetto del Tronto, CIHEAM Bari and **Ca' Foscari University of Venice**.* **An institutional register, not a hobby page** — and it classifies the pier as immovable material cultural property.

**⚠ What this archive already had, and what it still lacks.** *This is **not new**: [/searched/](/searched/) has carried it since September under «Defranceschi bridge, Rijeka», which established that **there is no bridge — there is a pier**, formerly **Mol Zichy**, and two things the register itself does not say:* **the first iron-and-concrete building in the port went up on it in 1882**, and **the first electric light in Rijeka was lit on it** — *by **Zipernowsky**, with lamps borrowed from the Torpedo Factory.* **What no source says is who the De Franceschi was.** *Until today that question sat in a search log with no worklist row behind it, which is why it has not moved.*

**Searched 28 September 2026 and nil, with the terms named:** *on the [Portal Stare hrvatske novine](http://dnc.nsk.hr/Newspapers/Search.aspx) — **`Franceschijev` → 0**, **`Francescijev` → 0**, **`molo De Franceschi` → 0**. **`Zichy` → 1025**, but that is the Hungarian magnate family in political news and not the pier.* **The portal's runs mostly end about 1925**, so if the renaming is Italian-era or post-1945 it would not be there at all.
